article: A pharmacist is basically a specialist in medication, meaning they probably know more about medicines than some medical practitioners. They do so much more than dispense medicine, they also offer consults on use and dosage. They are also the last line of defence when it comes to drug interactions, especially when a patient is treated by numerous practitioners. And last but not least, they deserve a medal for being able to translate a practitioner's handwriting.,I'm a nurse in a hospital, and pharmacists do a lot. They dose medication for patients whose liver or kidneys aren't functioning properly (meaning they're not able to clear the meds out of their system like a usual person would) and dose especially toxic medicines based on lab results. Lots of meds my patients get come with a physician order stating "Pharmacy to dose" bc the pharmacists are experts in how the drug works in and is processed by the body. They figure out alternate ways of getting a medicine into a patient when the usual ways aren't working, like when the patient needs a pill but chokes on everything they try to swallow, or need an IV drug but don't have an IV for whatever reason, because they have the knowledge to compare different methods if the same drug or alternate drugs that can go in a different way. They also double check medicine compatibility and dosage, which seems like a computer could do, but gets complicated when you have patients on many drugs being used in non-standard dosages for different conditions. They also physically mix the drugs, which requires a lot of knowledge of the chemistry of the body in order to ensure the med is safe to give and being given correctly. They're also in charge of a lot of the facets of making sure med errors don't happen. Pharmacists are experts on the drugs, so the doctor can focus on treating the patient, instead of reinventing the wheel.','Canadian retail pharmacist here: - My main job is to "check" prescriptions that come my way to make sure they're accurate. My assistant 99 times out of a 100 is the one who types the prescription and counts the actual pills. Common physical things I catch are wrong doses (2.5 mg instead of 25mg), wrong drugs (doxycycline-an antibiotic to be avoided in pregnancy vs doxylamine a morning sickness pill) and illegal prescriptions (narcotic forgeries). Some trained technicians can perform this step but IMO the above are easier to spot with pharmacist training. - Check prescriptions for "drug related problems" such as interactions. In my experience, pharmacists tend to be overly cautious people. So yes, we will run certain drug combos through our computer, or glance at the patient hand-out to "double check" ourselves-this is a good thing. Sometimes I need to remind myself of a drug I haven't seen in a long time! Once we get the information we can interpret its severity quickly, which a lay person could not. As others have pointed out, there are tons of interactions that get "flagged" and a pharmacist is able to determine which is important based on the individual patient. For example, I have prevented very serious problems by contacting doctors over a dangerously high dose of antibiotics in a child, or a drug interaction that was only meaningful because it was for a frail elderly lady. This is a pharmacist's job-doctors are trained for diagnosis, not drug interactions. - I help people understand their medications. For example, the man who just had a heart attack and is leaving the hospital overwhelmed with a pile of meds. Without me they usually will stop taking one or two (or go back to smoking, or try a over-the-counter snake oil instead) and be at risk for a second heart attack. I sit down with them, and based on their personal needs talk about the risks vs benefits of the meds. Then I call them in a few days and follow up, making sure they've made an appointment with their family doctor. Or, I do a medication reconciliation with an elderly woman who has too many medications with side effects, and work with her doctor to see if some can be stopped. - I answer people's questions 24 hours a day with more accuracy and clarity than google. (We are open extended hours) For example- its 2 AM and someone comes in with a sick child: what medication do they use? Should they go to the ER? This saves the healthcare system (or you, if you're American) money. - I give flu shots which saves the government money as they pay us less than doctors, and the patient time. I also give other vaccinations, such as hepatitis B, so if you're going to Mexico you can be protected without the need for extra doctor visits. - I prescribe certain medications for minor conditions, again saving the healthcare system money and the patient time. - I can change some prescriptions with the patient's ok, for example if a product isn't available or something is missing from the prescription. - I specialty make a lot of drugs, for example certain seizure medication for children isn't sold in liquid form- I will make this for you at 3AM when you realize you are completely out of doses for your kid. - I dispense and monitor methadone, helping former addicts come off narcotics and re-integrate back in society (in partnership with their awesome nurses.) - I deal with insurance agencies to try to get medications covered, sometimes contacting your doctor to see if an alternate drug would be acceptable. - I consult on the phone with doctors, nurses, homecare workers etc deciding what course of action would be in the best interest of the patient. - I use math calculations to be able to figure out the correct dose of things like Tylenol for infants too small to be listed on the box, again at 2 AM. Or help someone self-adjust their insulin. - I get annoyed when someone is yelling at me from across the counter wondering why their order isn't done yet, asking what the heck I do all day.;) TL;DR: Pharmacist's are drug therapy experts who can help you take charge of your health and decide if a certain medication is right for you. Like any profession there are a few dumblazy ones out there- but most of us work our butts off to keep you safe!', "Pharmacists are experts in medications, even more so that doctors. Doctors are responsible for a lot of information and decisions, done quickly. Under those circumstances, it can be easy to order medications that are incompatible in the same patient. One of their chief responsibilities is to make sure medication orders make sense, drug interactions are minimized, doses are appropriate, and so on. That makes it sound like they're only purpose is to doublecheck Dr.'s work, but in truth they tend to have a much more in-depth knowledge of the field of medications, their effects, and their doses. There's a lot more to it than that. The stuff you see them doing is counting to make sure the right number of pills get into your prescription. It gets much more difficult when there are multiple prescriptions on the same patient. Also sometimes doctors need doses that don't exist in pill form. In these cases it's up to the pharmacist to make a new pills, or capsules, or syrup liquids, in order to make the doses precise. For example, let's say there is an antibiotic that is only available in 200 mg tablets. A doctor needs syrup made up to give to a baby that has 75 mg in 1 teaspoon. A pharmacist has the technical expertise and know how to mix the syrup with the pills that are available. They really are an indispensable part of the care team.," "Makes sure that your Doctor isn't asleep or overworked by checking for interactions. Providing a ton of free advice about what cream for this rash or that minor condition you may have. Teaching about generics which might save you money. Calling your Doc and working out an alternative prescription which IS covered under your health insurance.," "Pharmacists assume I'm an idiot and view all of my prescriptions as pending death certificates for my patients. And, I can't be more pleased about it. Everyone makes mistakes. Even doctors. Pharmacists have saved my patients from my mistakes many times.,My pharmacist has saved my life a couple of times. I take a medication every day that doesn't play nicely with other drugs. When my doctor prescribes me something else like an antibiotic or an anti-inflammatory, even though she always checks her computer for interaction issues with my main meds, I still always double-check with the pharmacist. More than a few times he's had to call my doctor and say "oh hell no" and recommend a different drug. His knowledge of medications, uses and interactions is on a different level from my doctor's. Her focus is in diagnosis. So the two work together in concert very well.','Pharmacy technician here, They check that the prescription has been written correctly, that the patient can take the drug, i.e. is not allergic to something in it or that any other medications they take can be taken with the drug, and that the dispensed drug is correct. They also answer any questions that the patient has about the medication','Typically they counsel patients on proper dosage, potential side effects, any adverse issues when used in conjunction with other drugs, and recommend generics when available.', "I have to say that my pharmacist is a great guy. I get multiple scripts. Some are mail order through the Caremark, which CVS pharmacy is a part of. Carmark CONSTANTLY fucks up my orders. It becomes a big deal when I ordered my daughter's insulin 2 weeks ago and we are down to the last of it, and the mail order assholes still say it will be another 2 days. Sure I can get it at the CVS directly but it will cost 250 for one vial. This is when Dave, the pharmacist of the year, takes over. He called Carmark, chewed them out, got them to cover the cost of the temp vial due to it being their screw up, and there was no charge. Caremark has fucked up about 90 of any mail order scripts I have ordered. I have gone weeks without my blood pressure meds due to their screw ups. It is one thing to deal with high blood pressure, but quite another when your young kid is T1 diabetic. Thanks Dave! You are awesome and make my life easier.,From what I know, as far as the medical profession goes, we actually know very little about most medications. Pharmacists are the ones who understand and help research this stuff. It's a growing field and they have a serious education behind them. If it helps, think of the pharmacist as a medical teams reference for meds. There are tons of intricacies to medications that we have discovered (by accident) and use to our advantage, like the anti depressant effects of anti seizure medications (among others). Pharmacists do look after the rights of patients when dispensing a medication (right time, dose, frequency, person, medication, etc etc) but they're also monitoring those meds for rate of consumption (for those elderly patients who may forget to refill, or those patients at risk for addiction or abuse), they repackage into blister packs for people with arthritis or meter out small amounts for patients at risk of overdosing. There are intimacies to mixing up creams for fungal infections vs steroids for massive bacterial infections. These are the people who make the final warnings to avoid things like making sure you're not on oral birth control while taking antibiotics. If "It's a Wonderful Life" taught us anything, pharmacists have had to evolve a long way from keeping all the different white powders in jars along the same shelf. People probably die a lot less.', "pharmacists also deal a lot with insurance companies. getting drugs covered that would otherwise not be covered or have a very high copay, they obtain prior authorization for medications as well, get things overridden. things the patient is not going to be able to do. I worked at a pharmacy and the pharmacists there did a ton of interaction with insurance companies. also, before the wave of electronic scripts, pharmacies busted a lot of fraudulent prescriptions. I worked at a small locally owned pharmacy, places like that attracted a lot of fraudulent Rxs and it was pretty easy to spot a fake. e.g., a doc wrote for X medication 50 mg let's say. then the patient would put a 1 before the 50 but not in the exact same pen as the doctor did. or, a patient either obtained a doctor's script pad or the doctor was just in on it, doctors office was 50 miles west. pharmacy 50 miles east of the doc office and patient lived 50 miles east of the pharmacy. red flag right there.," "Think of your doctor as the waiter of a fine dining establishment. They suggest the wine to go with your dinner, and you can tell them what you like or what you need, and they will make sure you get taken care of. The pharmacist is the guy who actually prepares the food correctly, makes sure it's safe, and that you are getting what was ordered. There are many different doses for common medications and some of them don't come ready to dispense but instead have to be mixed on site by the pharmacist. The doctor who prescribed the drug is the expert on it's affects on the patient. And the pharmacist who fills the prescription is an expert on the drug itself, how it's dispensed, the dangers of the drug, possible interactions with other drugs, how to safely dispense the drug, etc. A pharmacist is a specialist in drugs and medications including preparation, dispensing, and safety, even more so than your doctor is.," "I have multiple health issues and when I am sick we call our pharmacist and the doctor around the time for treatment advice. I can't always see the same doctor in my group but I can talk to the same pharmacist.

article: Your router is running software, just like a small computer. Sometimes that software gets stuck, freezes up, etc. A reboot will reset the software to a good working state, and ensure the memory, cache, and other scratch space is clear. It will also free up any hung processes or things that could be slowing you down.','It would work even better if you turned it off and on.','I realize there is a grammar issue with this post.','I was a broadband tech support supervisor for 7 years. First off, you have the ISP (internet service provider), and they provide the signal via the cable network (aka. plant). That signal has a series of flags on it, two of the more well-known flags are DHCP (alternates your IP address based on a random protocol, and is network-based), and lease. One thing to realize is that, gateways aside, the modem (cable bridge) and the router are two separate objects that do different things. The modem is what talks to the network, and receives the information. The router takes that signal, encrypts it via NAT, and evenly distributes it through your network, either wired or wirelessly depending on your router. If you have an issue with your internet, and you reset your router, chances are that you are NOT going to fix your problem. This is why: Your modem has an IP address provided by the network, known as an external (or public) address. If you have a router, the router will request that IP like a computer would. The router than takes it, and hides it behind its own security (NAT). It will then provide all connected devices with another IP address, known as internal address. This is typically what you see when your address says 192.168.0.1, or something similar depending on where your device is in your network. When your router turns on for the first time, it will request the IP address from the modem. Although typically automatic, you can request the router to check with the modem periodically to make sure the IP address hasn't changed, but sometimes it doesn't work. If your modem's lease expires but isn't provided a new IP address, if there was a software update that wasn't properly applied to the modem, or if the modem is having a fault due to improper signal levelpacket loss, then the router may not get the updated information. Your computer will request information from the router, who then requests it from the modem. If the router and modem have conflicting information, the request is denied and you will get errors like "ISP unavailble" or "internet connection not detected" or "webpage unavailable." Now, if the problem is on the modem's end, resetting the router will not fix anything as it will still have the most updated information that the modem can provide. Resetting the modem may fix that, or you may need to call your ISP so they can adjust the information being sent. However, if the problem is on the router's end (ie. the router isn't requesting updated information), then resetting the router will force it to do its initial startup check, of which includes requesting new information. If the problem is not solved with that, and the modem is indeed fine, you may need to perform a factory reset on your router to clear any potentially bad firmware updates, or glitches.', "Sometimes a switch is flipped incorrectly internally and capacitors hold it in place. When you turn off the router, the capacitors discharge their stored energy and the switch is released. Then you turn it back on and everything works again because the switch was reset. EDIT: Why was this downvoted? The transistor is a switch that represents a 1 or 0. In a holding circuit, it is held in place by an electrical current. When that current is removed, it resets to the 0 state. This is essentially what the 1 comment said except that mine uses more broad layman's terms.," "As most people have said it can clean out any software issues as well as re-acquiring an IP address. However, something that only uWherearemylegs has said, and got wrongly downvoted for, is that it also has a hardware side. As well as resetting the software, it also clears out any charge stored in capacitors or other components. That's why they often tell you to switch it off wait 5-10 seconds and switch it back on; it takes that long for the capacitors to lose their charge.,When you leave your router on it can take up extra RAM and slow and sometimes disconnect your internet by turning off your modem it deletes all the extra ram build up and so you have a faster internet speed thus it turns or reconnects your internet

article: Senior reactor operator here. You withdraw the control rods. The control rods absorb neutrons needed for the reaction, so when you take them out, the neutrons are allowed to start interacting. You slowly withdraw the control rods and watch the neutron counts increase on your monitors. If the reactor is still offline after withdrawing a control rod, the neutron counts slowly increase then steady out. When enough control rods are withdrawn to bring the reactor supercritical, the counts will continue to exponentially increase. Operators monitor the reactor doubling time, or the reactor period. The doubling time is how long it takes for power to double. When the reactor is supercritical, the doubling time is constant, and power keeps exponentially increasing until it's high enough to heat the fuel up. When the power level is high enough to start heating the fuel, this is called the "Point of Adding Heat," and the temperature increase in the core causes the power level to stabilize. The reactor returns to exactly critical, and is now self sustaining. Power stops going up or down, it just sits steady. At this point operators will slowly withdraw rods to continue heating up the core, start producing steam, and start bringing the steam side of the plant online.', "Load the fuel rods with the control rods in place, and the reactor won't start to go critical until you start withdrawing the control rods.

article: It was a late winter afternoon when I walked up to the old seafood restaurant. The sun hung over the too wide and too straight road out front like I always remembered, but something about it seemed wetter and yellower than before. For years this was the place where everyone went to eat with their families after their shift at the factory or the plant or the mill or the smeltery. It was a sprawling two story building with walls of wet brown shingles. The second floor was smaller than the first floor and stood like a tower. I never knew what was up there. Still don't. Probably just a glorified storage shack and where the cooks do their blow. Now hard figures lingered outside, wrinkled faces with their Members Only jackets and 30 year old haircuts. The dads of ages gone by. They sucked in their cigarettes in with their chests as they looked off to nowhere in particular. The air here used to feel like sand. A car assembly plant, a steel mill, a plastics manufacturer, chemical plants and an asphalt mixery used to fill the air here with fumes that could almost choke the life from your lungs. But somehow it smelled like home. Now the only smell that blew in was the brackish odor of the tar from the asphalt plant. I walked past two women arguing in the local tinny drawl as I entered the door. Ronny stood at the decades old host's pulpit like he swore he'd be. "Mark!" he shouted as I walked in the door. "Hey buddy! Good to see you!" Mark came out from behind his station to give me the biggest hug I'd ever had from him. "I'm sure you love California, but life's been quiet here without you bro." I knew he was referring to his life minus one of his best and wildest friends, but I couldn't help but thinking he meant the restaurant. Three quarters of the tables were empty and neatly set. Ten years ago at that time of day, every table would have been seated while waiters all but ran between them with trays filled with crab cakes, raw oysters, rockfish, and bushels of crabs. The only thing that remained of that old scene was the odor of seafood and Old Bay that permeated the wood of which that house was built. The few people who were here were mostly old and had probably been eating here for decades. We chatted for a few minutes before I said, "What's with the wax museum dude?" Ronny looked hurt. "What do you mean?" "Everyone here is old." "So what?" "I don't know. It's just..... weird I guess." I don't remember most of the argument that followed. I remember that it was loud. I remember that before I stormed off Ronny said, "Well not all of us can run away to California like you! We might not be shiny but we're real!" What I remember more than the argument was that almost no one in the nearly silent dining room looked up from their meals to see the fracas at the door. Everyone just silently ate. And that was why I left five years ago.

article: To be completely honest, I never thought I would see this day come. Sure, crazy people on the corner of city streets would constantly preach about it day in and day out. And yeah, I heard the news stories lately about the rapidly degrading conditions of Earth. But c'mon. If someone told me yesterday that the world was 100 going to end, I would have told them that they were a silly goose who hadn't yet stepped outside to see what a beautiful day it was. That's what really threw me off. It was an absolutely gorgeous day yesterday! The sun was shining, not a cloud in sight. The Earth smelled green and new. Today was no exception. It was a normal Spring day. I woke up at my normal morning time 9 AM. I poured myself my normal cup of joe in my normal "I Heart Pugs" mug. Everything was so..... normal! It wasn't until a giant crack split my neighbor's house in half that I realized anything was wrong. To be honest though, Bobby was planning on moving out within the month anyway. It wasn't like he was in it when it happened. Thank God! Gee, that would have been truly disastrous. Anyway, so everyone began screaming in the streets. The sun was still shining above. Not a cloud in sight. The weather was breezy and beautiful as ever. The cracks in the ground were pretty darn deep, but then again we live in California. We should be used to earthquakes, right? Well I got ta admit, it was a bit excessive. So I grabbed up my little dachshund, Scoobs, and packed up my car with only the necessities since we were in a bit of a rush. I zoomed on down the street. I had offered Barbara a ride when I passed her house, but she was too frantic. I hadn't seen her this frazzled since the Black Friday Target fiasco of 2005. I continued on my way down to my favorite bar. I checked in to see if Lou was alright. He was pretty crazed too. The TV was ranting about all of this insanity being the Apocalypse or something. I didn't really pay it too much mind. I tried to calm a very distraught, sobbing Lou. He refused to move from behind the bar. I sighed and decided it best to keep on driving. If this truly was the "End of Time," then I thought it would be nice to take a scenic route so I can pass by the beaches. It would've been such a shame to pass up the opportunity considering it was such a beautiful day. I called my family members while driving. All of them were hysterical. I reassured them that even if this was the end, we all loved each other and that's all that really matters. Plus, we got to go on a wonderful family cruise last summer that visited the European countries of Greece, Italy, and Turkey. I very much believe that it healed our family in a lot of ways. Knowing that we have those precious memories makes up for not being together right now. Oh my, I better finish writing this little entry. You see, I've been an optimist about this whole ordeal. I've really believed that this would all pass. However, there is a quite terrifying tsunami headed my way as I type this. Not to mention, I passed many a house on fire and a few out of place tornadoes. My drive yesterday eventually led me here, a secluded beach somewhere in Northern California. I found a little shack and decided to write a little bit before kicking the bucket. Now although my optimism may be frowned upon by some possibly many, I must let you the reader understand that I was never completely shielded from reality. I knew there was a good chance that this really was the end. I only kept my hope alive because it would ensure, perhaps, a happier and more tranquil death. I am no fool. Death is an inevitable part of life. I am just content that I got to drive down this gorgeous Californian coast on a beautiful Spring day, got to call my family and tell them I love them, and got to find this quaint beach the last place I will ever visit. Here I have spent my last moments documenting my experience in the last 24 hours with a view like no other and my dog by my side. The wave is quite high now. Wow. Look at it! Must be a thousand stories high! Slightly sad now that I couldn't be on the coast of Hawaii or some other island. The water would have probably been a lot bluer and clearer! Oh well. You win some and you lose some. Ah! So my optimism remains! Even with this impressive wave about to consume me and Scoobs. A wise man by the name of Plato once said, "We can easily forgive a child who is afraid of the dark; the real tragedy of life is when men are afraid of the light." I can't say for sure Plato is talking about the afterlife. I was never the smartest cookie in the cookie jar. However for the purpose of my tale, I believe that is indeed what he is talking about. My optimism has allowed me to reject this idea of fear. I am excited for the light. I welcome it. In my head, I am waving farewell to you reader with the tune "Goodbye Stranger" playing in the background. Real cinematic like. I'll see you on the flip side, friend.

Chlorine, which is a negatively charged ion, can help balance the positively charged sodium and potassium ions in the tissues, which can promote healing and lessen pain. article: Brian Lindale cursed at his wife's dogs, like he did every day. Except this time, when he told the purebred Yorkshire terrier to "Die like the rat you are," he meant it. He could deal with the smell they built up over spending hours in their kennels, or the 2am barking that would spark the others to echo that sharp yipping. He even managed to somehow forgive when the smallest one chewed through the power cables on his 66" flat screen television, right when he really needed to just sit and watch something distracting for an hour. But now, images of drowning the animals in their swimming pool were tempted to stay in his mind's eye. Hell, he'd even bury them afterwards, which would be more then they deserve. He hated them especially today because now instead of leaving the house five minutes early, he would be leaving just on time. He checked the clock on his phone. 7:00. Takes twenty minutes to get there, interviews at 7:30. I'll be fine he hoped. Brian carried their kennels to the back door and opened their little gates. He gagged at the smell, and realizing that there was shit even on the handles. He rushed to the kitchen sink to wash his hands immediately, using too much dish soap as he always did. Brian was the type of person who liked clean hands, and if they were ever dirty at some point in the day, he would feel anxious. And even worse, Brian bit his nails down to the flesh, so he had to be extra careful to avoid situations like these. Scrubbing that bit of brown on his hand that just wouldn't come off, he looked up to find the dogs playing with each other, covering their white fur with shit and piss. He looked over to his phone. It showed only a black screen. Brian nudged the front button with his elbow and it showed 7:03. Ill be fine He stepped over the kennels to get to the backyard, careful not to swing the door open too much so the little rats couldn't scurry inside. He scolded them as they tried to jump on his legs. "Shoo, you little shits. Get the fuck away from me." He managed to get to the side of the house, walking barefoot over their white rock landscaping, peppered with bits of dry dog shit. He evaded them all and got to the green hose the gardeners used to water their four palm trees. He traced the hose to its source and turned the spout. He held the hose up, and chilling cold water dribbled out from the tip. He held his thumb on it, but there wasn't enough pressure to make a spray. Brian had to trace the hose again to find where it had folded, and found it on the third try. The pressure inside the hose finally let out, spraying water straight into the air. Now he had dirty water on him, but he didn't care. After this, he would need to shower again anyway. He held his thumb to the tip and sprayed the hose water at the dogs. Of course, they took him for playing and tried to jump at him. If his wife saw him repelling the little rats now by spraying directly into their faces, she would be livid. They misbehave because they know you hate them! she would say. It was the kind of thing that he thought was cute when she said it, but thinking on it later would just irritate him. What kind of sense does that make? Shitting on yourself must be some protest When finally they were as white as their innocent little souls, Brian ushered them into their spare kennels. Of course, the last one never wanted to go back in once he had been let out. But like Brian, we don't all get what we want. He carried their now full kennels inside, trying not to let their yipping get on his nerves. He set them down, walked back to the kitchen sink and checked his phone. 7:08. I'll be fine The shower was nice, at least. He liked his showers hot enough to fog the mirrors. But he didn't have the time to stew in it long. He jumped out, toweled off and slipped into his extra suit. As he walked out the door, he checked his phone. 7:15 If I hurry, I'l be fine Brian powered on his GPS device, and waited anxiously for his directions. Suddenly the screen went dark. Dead? No not now He pressed the power button desperately, but nothing else happened. "Damn NSA" he said aloud. The National Security Agency years ago made a deal with global phone providers to record all audio around every cellular device, and to shut down phones before all power was depleted in order to maintain recording. At least, that's what he had heard. He cursed the NSA out of habit, but also to try and make light of this awful situation. Brian certainly remembered where he was going: for a job interview at the local paper to write a sports column. The press factory for the Reno Times was the largest building in town, outside of North Virgiinia Street. Damn near every schoolboy in the city worked as their paperboys back in the 60s, when he grew up. Times were simpler then. Dogs stayed outside, phones didn't die and employers understood if you had a bad morning coming in. But now, companies just dont care. With one of every seven people unemployed, the companies could be as hard as they wanted on their workers. What would they do, quit? Good luck feeding your family. It was a kind of leverage that would be called criminal, back when Brian grew up. Now it's just good business. He checked his phone again to check the time. Still dead. No idea how late I am Nervously he looked at his hand, and found the nail on his right pinky finger just a bit longer than the others, showing the tiniest sliver of white at the tip. He bit down, remembered his cleaning work that morning, and gagged. He spat outside his window. Best not to think about it. Think about the road, we got ta hurry on Brian backed out of the driveway and went. The kids were on summer break, so there wouldn't be any pedestrians running about trying to catch busses or chase playballs. He remembered almost hitting a child while he was checking his phone for the time. He remembered the panic, a kind of trance you enter where everything can go wrong and your mouth tastes like metal. But seeing no pedestrians around, he sped out of his home. While driving, you always believe you're hitting every red light. Like a man in a traffic control tower is looking at you, making sure the yellow light comes on just far enough away to make you doubt yourself. But now he was certain of it. Brian passed by Piggy Pete's Coffee, which was really just a donut shop with week old coffee. This was the type of place that stayed open until 11pm so the city's hipsters could eat donuts snobbily, if that were a thing. He remembered being a kind of social rebel back then, insisting that his friends listen to the Stones instead of the Beatles, and before that Beatles instead of Elvis. But only the young have time for that now, and certainly not Brian. Traffic slowed to a crawl, and Brian cursed aloud. "Are you fucking kidding me, what now?" He nudged his car to the right so he could look ahead. A quarter mile ahead, on the side of the road, a red minivan had sideswiped a green honda. It was always the green hondas. It's like people who can't drive gravitate to cheap cars they can use up and throw away. But what bothered Brian was that everyone wanted to slow and see what was going on. He wasn't the kind to nose into other people's business, especially one so boring as a traffic accident. But sure enough, every single person driving by bneeded to slow and inspect it. And once they had, they revved up to meet the normal Reno driving speed: Speed Limit 10. When he had finally broken free of the slump, he reached that certain Reno Go, everyone in a rush to get nowhere. Except he had to rush to the Reno Times, and now he finally saw their large sign just around the I-580. Reno Times it flashed. 7:35pm he panicked. August 5th Don't Text and Drive He raised his fingernails to bite them, remembered the smell of shit, and grimaced. He looked down at his hand for a second and found it: a dab of dog dung on his wrist. Somehow he missed it while washing. Oh god, what if I went into the interview like this He looked up at the road again and found the RT Drive exit coming, where he would need to turn off. Suddenly the smell of shit was giving him immense anxiety. He would need to wash it off now. Brian turned the wheel toward the exit, and started steering the wheel with his knees. He leaned over to the glove box where he kept a small stack of napkins. He pulled one out and wiped off his wrists, looking up at the road every half second to make sure he was still in his lane.He finally wiped his wrist clean when the wheel sllipped over his knee. He quickly grabbed the wheel, napkin still in hand. "GOD FUCKING DAMN IT" He let go of the hand holding the napkin and it stuck to the steering wheel, held in place with wet dog shit. He rolled down the windows to let out the smell as he turned into the Reno Times parking lot. He came to the end of a line at parking validation, each driver waiting their turn to get a ticket. Come on, come on. Get your fucking ticket already he cursed to himself, realizing the absurdity of what he said but he didn't care. These people needed to hurry up. Now.

article: At first, we thought it was something thrown out of the asteroid belt, hurtling towards earth at thousands of miles a second. Some said the apocalypse was neigh, most hoped it would be caught by the moon, like most large asteroids. We were all surprised when it entered a stable high altitude orbit well away from the orbits of any of the thousands of satellites orbiting the earth at the time. It was rectangular, made of uniform gray metal, and roughly the size of an apartment building. It was like nothing we've ever observed in space, before or since. The really surprising thing, when you think about it, is that it took us three whole weeks to send a ship out there to investigate. When the astronauts arrived they found that it was covered in writing. Hundreds of languages, all spoken here on earth, repeating over and over and over again. The message was simple. " We are sorry, but you are alone. " Your Earth was the last known planet in the galaxy to develop intelligent life. It was decided long ago to allow a species to develop to interstellar travel before being contacted by the galactic government. Unfortunately, we've been forced to contact you sooner rather than later. " There has been a disaster. " By the time this reaches Earth humanity will be alone in the galaxy. We are sorry not to have known you, but if we had you would have been gone alongside us. " For your species sake, do not venture beyond your own solar system. Exploration is a basic tenant of intelligent life. Unfortunately you must cut your exploration short. " Stay in your stellar nursery. If you do so you will at least survive, if not thrive. At the time no one knew what to make of that message. That there had been other life in the galaxy all but the most crazed of conspiracy theorists believed to be true. But the rest of it? Some took the aliens at their word; something catastrophic happened that wiped out all life in the galaxy except for us. Others distrusted the aliens, believing they were trying to keep us from becoming a threat. Most of us weren't sure what to think, but we've been cautious. Its been nearly 600 years since that hunk of steel began to orbit the Earth. 600 years. For the last 100 of those years we've been chomping at the bit, wanting to reach for what we've been told will harm us. There is a second thing written by those aliens that is absolutely true. Exploration is a tenant of intelligent life. Humanity can no more survive without it than we could survive without oxygen. And so, on this historic day, we send a ship to do that thing we've been doing since the day we first climbed down from the trees. We are going to explore.

article: They aren't powers of 360. They are multiples of 360. A power of 360 would be represented as 360720," "It makes scaling between them simpler. For some time, for the sake of backwards-compatibility, it's best to scale old content up rather than re-master it. Think of a tiny picture with 2x2 pixels. And two new displays with 3x3 pixels and 4x4 pixels. To scale the image up to the 4x4 display is simple enough. Just repeat each pixel twice. But the 3x3 will be a pain. If you repeat the first pixel, but not the second since you can't, the image will stay sharp but distort. If you count the average from neighboring pixels and fill the extra pixels with that, the image won't distort but won't be sharp either. Or you can keep the 2x2 image and fill the rest with black bars. A 5x5 display would similarly sucks but 6x6 would be sweet again. I'm only using small numbers to make up a worst-case scenario. It all kind of blends in the mass when the resolutions are in the thousands. But it's still noticeable. To see what I mean in real-life, for a distorted image, try setting a 4:3 resolution in your 16:9 monitor. Everything will stretch wider. And for blurry image, try setting a resolution that's close to your display's native resolution but not exactly it. For example 1050p for 1080p display. Depending on how your monitor handles things, it may add the black bars or do the averaging thing. These you are more likely to find in-OS. On third-party applications that allow custom resolutions, it's possible to find even better (or worse) examples. So to scale up a 720p image to 1080p they have the option of repeating every other pixel. It's not optimal, but keeps the image similar enough. Same goes for 1080p to 1440p. from 1080p to 4k it's again repeating every pixel. From 720p to 1440p it's repeating every pixels. And of course, if the content is specially made for 1440p or 4k, it'll be pristine on those displays and to scale down to 1080p or 720p, they leave out pixels.,Modern Computer resolutions inherited their display sizes from a legacy of punch cards and the number of scan lines of cathode ray tubes. You see the original graphics resolution for PCs was VGA with 640x480 and most of the ones that came later like like SVGA (800x600) were based upon that. The VGA inherited the resolution from text based resolution where you did not display graphics but rather charters in for example an 80 by 25 or 80 by 60 grid. If you have an 80x60 grid and use 8by8 pixels per character you arrive at the original VGA resolution. The 80s characters per line is something far older that modern computer displays. IBM standardized on punch cards with 80 columns in 1928. So the whole 80 characters was sort of inherited from those type of equipment (also 72 characters were often used with teletypes for practical reasons.) This sort of gave you the horizontal resolution increments we still use to day. The vertical ones from your question came thanks to the combination of wanting nice square characters that were 8x8 pixels in the beginning and the whole thing being compatible with American TV screens which were based on NTSC which had 480 scan-lines. Early home computers used TVs as their display. So that was the limit they could use. Originally TVs were not digital like today but analogue. They did not have any pixels just a ray of electrons that wandered back and forth and down from the bottom across as specially made glass surface making it glow. Horizontally they theoretically did not have any resolution at all, but vertically it was divided into rows upon rows that they ray moved along. The original design used in the US had more than 480 of these, but not all of them were visible and in the end 480 were only used of what remained to get a nice round number. We have long since moved away from all the thing these values originally came from, but the steps to go from where we started tow here we ended up were all small and all were taken in mind with the idea of staying compatible with what came before.','It has less to do with "360" and more to do with the aspect ratio. article: So, I haven't given this too much thought, and my goal here is to tease out the various arguments. But my essential point is that it seems to me that representative democracies like the USA, Europe or Canada... suffer from over reliance on representatives. Systematically, using a third party representative to advocate your civic needs is a lot like relying on an insurance company to advocate your interests when you go to the hospital. They have generally aligned interests, but they can suffer from serious conflicts that make them unable to truly represent the peoples' needs. In the economy, we are told that the way to adjust for this problem by allowing for more competition from the actual user of the health services. Similarly, in democracy, we need more direct democracy to help keep the representatives in check. this is particularly important in times of gridlock or when a serious question is at hand. I disagree with the decision of the people of Scotland in not becoming independent, but I think that their ballot question was extremely important for keeping the system in check. Similarly, the USA needs to implement more direct democracy. Let the people decide whether there should be immigration reform. whether taxes should be raised... not every time, but often enough to make a difference. The fundamental problem with representative democracy is that you elect a bunch of crusty old men (except in Scandinavia) who say one thing while campaigning, and do something else when elected. that or the you are forced to chose the "lesser of two evils" because you pick a candidate who supposedly has a position on every issue under the sun when you only care about a couple. this candidate can't care about or know much about most issues, and you can't care of know much about all issues, so it is extremely unlikely that you and the representative you vote for will actually have all that much alignment when they become your representative. The way to solve this is by allowing the people to actually decide issues from time to time. Allow the public some ability to rank where they want their taxes spent, rather than leaving it all up to lobbyists to decide in smoky back rooms... article: An important factor to note is something called hydroplaning. Hydroplaning is what happens when water can't get out from underneath a tire fast enough, and the tire slips on top of this water, instead of touching the pavement. Smooth tires grip the best on smooth pavement because they have the most contact, but will be prone to hydroplaning, because the water has nowhere to go. article: Heartburn is the colloquial term for gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). Your stomach has two "valves" at either end. At the top is the lower esophageal sphincter, this is the border between your esophagus (tube food goes down when you swallow) and stomach. Your stomach is lined with special cells that secrete mucous to protect themselves from acid. Heartburn occurs when stomach acid makes its way past this sphincter and begins to irritate the cells of the esophagus that do not have the special protective mucous layer. There are several different causes of heartburn, from bacterial infection (h. pylori) to insufficiency in the sphincter itself. To help alleviate the symptoms you can use over the counter antacids such as alka-seltzer and try to avoid laying down for several hours after eating (or if you must lay down, try to lay on your left side so gravity helps keep the acid in your stomach. For more severe and recurrent heartburn you should see a doctor and they'll give you medication to help prevent too much acid production (Histamine-2 blockers and proton pump inhibitors) or fight an h. pylori infection. GERD can be a very serious problem and I highly recommend you see a doctor if it is a regular problem for you. Continually irritating your esophagus with acid can cause strictures or a condition called Barrett's Esophagus which can lead to esophageal cancer.', "It's usually an excess of acid in your stomach. Or, your stomach is too full, and it's contractions push some of the digestive juices up into your esophagus. Or, if you're on your backright side, and the valve the closes your stomach off from the esophagus doesn't seal, some of your stomach acids can flow into your esophagus. I'm not going to claim this is the best explanation, but as a general idea it's good enough

They would also film the attention grabbing scenes first.', "Filming doesn't always go from beginning to end.,They pull things from the partially or mostly edited film to cut them into the trailer. Sometimes producers will even make sure certain scenes get cutgradedsoundetc. first so that they can be used in the trailer.','There are lots of reasons movies are delayed even after they are finished. The people who own the movie want to see it make the most money possible, and so they look ahead at all the movies that are coming up and they try to decide on the best time to launch their movie. Imagine that their movie is a space epic, and there are two more space epics being launched next week. These movies are competing for the same audience, and many of them can only afford to watch one. The owners of our space epic might be able to make more money if they wait until those other ones are out of the theater before launching their movie. If there are no other space epics in the theaters, than fans of that genera will be less likely to skip it. Also, some types of movies are known to do better during certain seasons. There might be more money to be made by delaying the film until that season starts. Also, in order for a movie to maximize its profits, everyone needs to know about it. This is called marketing and building a good marketing campaign can take a long time - sometimes it takes even longer than it took to shoot and edit a film. This campaign needs to run for a long time before the movie comes out to build up interest, and sometimes movies are delayed to stretch out the advertising campaign and increase awareness.','The other answers here are pretty spot on. To expound a little bit, production of a film happens in stages. Sometimes these stages overlap, sometimes they're separated by a good deal of time. Every director does things a little differently in terms of how they organize filmings, location shoots, studio photography, and so on, but it's pretty typical to have a stage of "principal photography" where you go out and get all of the critical scenes of a movie shot. The director and other stakeholders then go into the studio and review all of this footage and put together a rough cut of the movie and see how well the story flows. Very often, this is enough footage for the trailer, even though the movie is no where near done. There's still a lot of work to do in terms of secondary, background, and studio photography to get the whole story to play out to the writer and director's visions, but there's already enough for a 30-90 second trailer by a wide, wide margin.','Often specific scenes are chosen to be edited first for early promotion, but the overall total post-production process can take months.

article: MD5 is not "encryption" so to speak. To figure out how MD5 works, imagine you have a collection of numbers. Let's say: 1, 2, 3, 5, and 10. MD5 can create a "hash" of data, but let's create a much simpler hash algorithm for our data. The simplest way to do this is to add up our numbers: 1 2 3 5 10 21. This is deterministic. No matter how many times we add those numbers we'll always get the same answer. But there's a problem: we can't go back to the original data, because although our numbers add up to 21, so do a lot of other numbers. If we hashed some other numbers, like 10 and 11, we would also get 21 just the same. This is called a "collision." All hashing algorithms have collisions. The tricky part of designing a secure hash algorithm is to allow for possible collisions, but to minimize their existence as much as possible. To be unique, but not too unique. As long as a collision is possible, it is impossible to figure out what the original data was. This is why hashes are called one-way encryption. You cannot go back. A more ELI5 explanation: Imagine a peach and a nectarine. We take both the peach and nectarine and squish them in a very specific way. Now we can't really tell which one was a peach or nectarine (this is called a "collision, but we do know that whenever we squish a peachnectarine in this way, we'll always get the same kind of mess every single time. This is a way to verify that the original object was indeed a peach, but we can't tell exactly what kind of peach it was, and we can't tell its original shapeskincolor either. This is how MD5 and every other hashing algorithm works. It takes data and mangles it deterministically to the point where it's unrecognizable and impossible to figure out what the original data was. The problem with MD5 is that there are too many collisions: it's too easy to get the same kind of mess from different pieces of fruit.

article: We know that numbers whose decimal representation terminate have certain properties. Specifically, if N terminates, there must be two integers, X and Y, such that X Y N. So if a number has a terminating decimal representation, it can be written as a fraction ab, where a and b are integers and b has only 2 andor 5 as prime factors (because those are the only prime factors of 10, the base of our decimal system). Conversely, if a fraction can be expressed as ab, where b has only 2 andor 5 as prime factors, then its decimal representation will terminate (i.e., it will end in a finite number of digits). For example, the fraction 725 can be written as a terminating decimal: 0.28. In this case, 25 has only 2 andor 5 as prime factors (25 52), so 725 can be expressed as a terminating decimal. On the other hand, the fraction 13 cannot be expressed as a terminating decimal, because its denominator (3) has a prime factor other than 2 andor 5. Its decimal representation is 0.333333..., which goes on forever. Hope this helps!

article: Escape velocity Life extension "escape velocity" is when we figure out how to extend life 10 years, but in that 10 years we learn how to extend life 15 years, and then with in that 15 we learn how to extend it 25 years. And this continues until we've mastered age. The escape velocisty is when life extension outpace the rate at which one's body dies. And these will not be decrepit lives at least eventually not hook to life support, but vital and vibrant. I believe most people will want this (except some group of religious people, but they'll die and be replaced by those who likely do want this). Demand While this will initially this will only be available for the rich, it's practically an inflexible demand: use it or die. Inflexible demands make a hell of a lot of money, and also generate a lot of political activism. Short of a totalitarian government that can contain and deny its citizenry the life extension, it seems very likely it will be used broadly. Once the economy of scale helps kick in, millions won't die. Then maybe a billion. The ever-changing population replacement rate If 75 of the population has their life effectively extended, then we need a birth rate of .5 per woman. As life extension improves, the birthrate has to reduce in tandem. If these millions or billions keep having children, even at a the low rates japan has right now 1.41 births per woman, the world will quickly begin filling up. Yes, western society has a declining birthrate, and yes, reducing infant mortality and increasing female education is significantly lowering the birthrate in developing countries. But this looks to be insufficient, as a birthrate of 2 per woman goes from being the replacement rate, to growth. So far, no western society has even neared a birthrate of .5, so we have no examples of this being sufficient motivator to prevent overpopulation. Eventuality Don't waste your time trying to convince me that we're actually going to keep dieing whether we figure this out in 20 years as some predict, or in 250, all of this still applies. Conclusion: human rights will change In the future, it seems to me that the Right to Life and the "Right to Children" will be in direct conflict, and that it seems both practical and inevitable that the Right to Life will be valued more highly. Therefore, I believe that we must sacrifice the "Right to Children," and implement for the good of society severe reproduction restrictions as soon as it is evident that life extension technology is outpacing aging. Jade hummed to herself as she pushed a steamer trunk up one of the city's gentle slopes. Foot traffic was low, as it usually was, the dead weren't in a rush to go anywhere, but occasionally she did stop and wave'hello' to a fellow pedestrian. A broad-shouldered man with a plumed hat and a blue petticoat, an old oriental hunched over his walking stick and clothed in vibrant reds and yellows; the occasional red-faced drunkard trying to convince himself that there was still something beating inside of his chest cavity. Very few of them returned her greeting. She did not allow their sullen faces to dampen her mood. She never thought of death as a loss, she thought of it simply as a transition. Of course, she was aware that the city was a poor place to live (if she could still use that word), with it's dreary decor and the lack of sunlight. But, what where the alternatives? Restless souls had tried to venture outside of it's boundaries in the past into the cracked, dry wastes beyond, with torches and improvised weapons in hand. It never amounted to much. Sometimes they would return, disappointed and maybe missing a few men. Other times they wouldn't return at all, swallowed by the darkness. The Authorities had prohibited expeditions outside of the city when the latter became more likely than the former. The cumbersome steamer trunk rolled onwards on a trolley that might've been blue once. Now it was only partially blue. The streets were filled with the sound of it's rubber wheels skidding on the uneven cobblestone. Jade was afraid that she might lose control or that the heavy leather belts strapping the trunk down might come undone. Fortunately, she made it without any unnecessary incidents. Her apartment was on the top floor of the Heffler building, which was four stories tall. The climb wouldn't have been much of a problem on it's own, however it seemed impossible for Jade's petite size. Nonetheless she released her hold on the trolley and stepped up to open the front door. It opened on its own, before Jade could reach the doorknob. "Uh, hello." said the young man standing in the door frame. He seemed to be a new arrival. You could always tell the newbies from the longtime dwellers. The smell of the city hadn't stuck to you yet. Jade blushed. He had a soft boyish face, but it was handsome nonetheless. "Hi," she replied, still a bit embarassed that he caught her unaware. The lad introduced himself as Wyatt and was, as predicted, a newcomer to Tres Morte. Jade told him that she had been here only two years herself. The truth was that she had been in the city for much longer, but if you start telling people that then they became much more prone to questions. "God," Wyatt said between gasps for breath, "How many more stairs?" "Just a few more! " , Jade giggled, standing ahead of Wyatt, just in case he dropped the steamer trunk. The gesture was cute, but Wyatt's thin, lanky frame didn't seem up to the task of climbing all those stairs lugging such weight. "If you need help, you could always ask!" "What do you keep in this? Bricks? " , asked Wyatt as the trunk bumped against another step. Just as they were nearing the top, the handle on the steamer trunk broke and it fell down the stairs. The lid broke on the previous landing and a man stumbled out. He ran down the stairs, mumbling through a dirty rag. Before Wyatt could react, Jade slid a dagger into the back of his throat. Blood soaked his shirt and soon dribbled onto the floor. Jade felt her heart flutter. She knew he wouldn't die. Nobody died in this place, but they could still feel. Jade knew that Wyatt felt every inch of that cold steel through his flesh and it made her quiver with joy. Wyatt gurgled something that might've been a scream. Jade cleaned the blade on Wyatt's shirt before sliding the slim, almost dainty little dagger into it's sheath under her petticoat. She didn't care that one of her toys ran from her. She had found something even better, though the wriggly little mouse would be likely to alert the Authorities to her location. She smiled. It would be a chase then. She was not new to evading the police, and Tres Mortes had so many nooks and crannies where she could hide.

article: You pretty much have it right. Brostep is a sub-genre of Dubstep, and Dubstep is much less specific. Really, the only requirements for something to be dubstep are to be bass-heavy, have a tempo between 130-150 BPM and have a distinct "wobble" bass sound. Dubstep also often incorporates elements of other genres such as hip-hop, reggae, and techno. Brostep, on the other hand, is a more aggressive and intense form of dubstep that emerged in the late 2000s. It is characterized by high-pitched and in-your-face bass drops, the use of heavy synths, and a focus on maximizing the energy of the track. Brostep is often criticized by purists as being too mainstream and lacking the depth and complexity of traditional dubstep. Overall, both genres have their unique qualities and are enjoyed by different audiences.

article: To quote Obama: "I think it's important to recognize that you can't have 100 security and also then have 100 privacy and zero inconvenience." I believe the type of security promised here is a fallacy. You'll always have "terrorists" conspiring against the state, but unless your goal is to monitor every single communication between two individuals (a la 1984), the conspirators will always be one step ahead, find ways around surveillance, and likely just become even more enraged by the oppressive lifestyle they're being forced to operate under. As Orwell puts it: "The choice for mankind lies between freedom and happiness." We're currently somewhere in the middle, where the government promises happiness, at the expense of some freedom, by spending billions on NSA projects which give the capability to monitor as much digital communication as possible. I think this effort is in vain, and a massive waste of taxpayer money - the only way it could be effective is if it were enacted as totally as in the dystopian future described in 1984 (where avoiding surveillance is much more than simply a minor inconvenience), which is obviously completely undesirable. Therefore we should probably just go back to the "freedom" end of the spectrum. tl;dr: Surveillance in the name of security is only worthwhile if it captures every single piece of communication. article: A few clarifications since I didn't want to clutter the title: - I say on the right, but that's because in America we drive on the right. If you live in a country where that's different, it might be more ideal to stick to the left. - I'm talking about informal pedestrian traffic such as entering and leaving a building. Something like crossing a street in the city where actual traffic laws apply would override this consideration. - I'm speaking from a perspective of efficiency, predictability and convenience, not legality. It would be silly to argue this should be enforced by any means outside of small social sanctions (a weird look or a sneer, for example.) - People who need to use automatic doors (wheelchairs, strollers, and so on) or places that force you to use a particular inout door also override this consideration (there's nothing you can do about the choice the venue has made.) I think there is a sort of social contract involved when walking to conform to certain norms. One of these is that people should stick to a particular side to avoid walking or bumping int other people, organize traffic, and avoid that awkward dance where you decide who gets to go first when two paths ultimately do collide. I chose the right because I live in America and it seemed like a natural application and, in my experience, most people are inclined towards walking on this side save for a few pedestrian rogues. Everybody making the conscious effort to stick to one side means shaving off a few seconds here and there by avoiding weird shuffles or knocking into other people. There's less awkward interaction every time two people aren't paying enough attention until the very last second. Sticking to a side creates (size permitting) a small 'passing gap' for people who walk a little faster than others rather than forcing a weird blend in the middle of people walking almost on the "wrong" side. article: Console pick a resolution and stick with it. If the target is 720p, the game will render at 1280x720 and upscale to 1920x1080 or downscale to 852x480. Games that have been scaled look like crap; PC gamers demand that games render at the native resolution of their monitor. Any game that doesn't is (properly) derided as crap. If there is only one resolution to render at, the designers can make a huge number of assumptions that greatly simplify development. Every user of a console game uses the same controller. The people that don't use that controller use a controller that emulates the normal controller. On the other hand, PC gamers not only demand that games work with whatever bizarre keyboard or speed pad or keypad or joystick they own, but they demand that the game allows buttons to be remapped to suit their similarly bizarre purposes. Ask 100 different WoW players what buttons do what and you'll get 150 different responses. Every console has the same CPU, the same video card, the same amount of RAM, the same storage medium, and none of them have any processes running in the background. If a game encounters a slowdown in a certain situation, the game will always slow down there on every single console owned by every single user every single time. You can then optimize that section or cut detail in that section. On the other hand, some PCs are CPU limited, some PCs are GPU limited, some PCs are memory bandwidth limited, some PCs are memory quantity limited, some PCs have more or less disk space or disk speed, some PCs have resident programs (malware, malware scanners, a browser that was left open with a flash animation running, crappy OEM software like picture organizers that are always running, the hideous monstrosity that is HP's printer suite) that sop up any given resource, and you typically can't predict the slow parts. You'll need to expose every detail setting to the user to enable them to configure it, and then you'll need to know when the user is a fucking moron and override some of their settings if you need to. Video cards from ATI and nVidia behave much differently. There are differences between each generation of video cards, sometimes drastic ones. You need a few different rendering paths, and need to pick the right one depending on what hardware is available. Consoles do not have this problem. Other devices can have similar problems (sound cards might perform certain functions slowly or at the use of a lot of CPU) and in all cases you need to be more tolerant of whacky inputs. PC gamers are, to varying degrees, tolerant of bugs at launch, console gamers are not. Console gamers are more tolerant of minor bugs that persist, PC gamers do not tolerate bugs that are not eventually fixed.," "It's like Italian, Japanese and Australian people are all people but they speak different languages. If the Australian wants to ask the Italian or Japanese person what time it is, they can do it by pointing at their watch because everyone will understand what is being asked and how to answer it. This is okay for simple questions but doesn't work so well for more complicated things. To be able to answer more complicated problems, the people can learn each other's language. To understand some things takes a bit of effort. By the time the Japanese person understands all of the Australian's strange phrases, they are practically Australian. An American or English person might find that easier because the language they speak is closer to start with. The different consoles, PCs, Macs and phones are all computers that understand different language. Some of the simpler things about them are often the same but the more complicated things they can do are often different.,Making games is like making tires for bikes, kinda. With consoles, everyone has the exact same bike, so the tire can be made for the bike. With PCs, everyone has slightly different bikes, different size tires, different gears, and sometimes they even have different numbers of wheels! The people who ride PC bikes want a tire to be perfect for every single bike, no matter how strange their specific bike may be.',' Take a 1 reddit (distance measurement) racetrack. For the Xbox and PlayStation the 1 reddit race track never changes. You can ride around on your bike a million times and you get to know all the small tricks of the racetrack. You can go really fast all the time. For the computer, the 1 reddit racetrack changes everytime you go on it. You may have a better bike that would like you pedal faster but since you do not know all the small tricks, you can not go as fast.','What about the code environment? article: Under US law if anything that is 5 calories or below it can be advertised as 0 calories. Another thing is that it can take energy to metabolize the food or drink which in all lowers the calorie count, like with celery.','Biochemist here. As someone mentioned, most things are advertised as 0 calories actually have some minuscule caloric content, but the FDA allows things to be less than 5 calories to be listed as 0 instead. This pertains to things like cooking spray, which is literally aerosol fat but its serving size is so small it is "practically" 0 calories. With regard to artificial sweeteners, lets use aspartame as an example. If you are familiar with organic chemistry and you take a look at its structure, you'll actually see that it's almost exactly a dipeptide of phenylalanine and aspartate, with a methyl ester on the phenylalanine. Coincidentally, this small compound of 2 amino acids causes a sweet taste instead of an expected proteinsavory one. However, like a proteinpolypeptide, it will digest into simple components of aspartate, phenylalanine, and accompanying methanol. The first 2 are normal amino acids and will be easily utilized by the body. The latter can actually form a toxic metabolite of formic acid, but since aspartame is potent in sweetening and therefore used in very small amounts in products, the amount that forms is negligible and not a concern unless taken in extreme excess. Other artificial caloric replacements usually work on the principle of having similar structures to activate "flavor" receptors but are modified enough so that they can't be targeted by human digestive enzymes. As a background, enzymes tend to have very specific substratestructure specificity, so just modifying the way 2 monomers are connected slightly or even just changing an alpha bond to a beta bond in a structure are enough to prevent the vulnerability to digestion. An example of nature of how specific enzymes can be can be seen in glucose polymers. Glucose polymers in alpha bond configurations are what most organisms digest for easy carbohydrate energy. FiberCellulose is exactly the same as those glucose polymers except they monomers are linked in beta conformation. These type of compounds (for the most part) just can't be metabolized and just go through unaffected. One humorous example one of my professors told me about was a artificial zero calorie fat they were attempting to use in potato chips. It was a compound of fatty acids with some modifications, most prominently attached to a carbohydrate. The structure was similar enough to trigger similar taste receptors but different enough to prevent digestion. A concern was, since the substance was still rather oily, that lack of digestion would cause the slick substance to build up and cause a leaky, well lubricated bowel in individuals that consume too much. "Clean Underwear" tests seemed to show the fear was unfounded, but I still have my doubts. When the body can't digest and utilize substances, they usually just pass through from one end to the other. If they are absorbed but are xenobiotics (organic structures that are not harmful but not beneficial either), CYP enzymes in the liver usually metabolize them to inert substances that are just passed through as well.', "They aren't. For instance water is 0 calories. It provides no energy. Most drinks are 95 water. So if you add things that don't get metabolized to produce energy, they can actually burn some calories since your body had to work to absorb it. For instance, vitamin C has flavor but few or no calories. Or stevia as an I gradient tastes sweet but cannot be digested. So our body just poops it out.

article: Basically people have lent these governments money and the governments can't pay them back. The governments would like to restructure their debt (in effect meaning the lenders get paid less). Lenders don't want to see the money they lent out go up in smoke and never get paid back, so they are attempting to sue those governments to prevent them from restructuring their debt.," "They buy debt very cheaply and then press for a settlement usually. They're patient, have lots of lawyers, and usually in the right (legally) so they can usually seize assets eventually and just about every nation has some assets outside their territory. Once that happens they'll usually get the settlement they want.," "It's like this: Company A invests 10 million in Puerto Greco and gets a bond in return. A little while later Puerto Greco gets in trouble and tells Company A they aren't going to get the 10 million back. Company A's bond is now pretty much worthless, but then Company B comes along and offers to buy it for 1 million. Company A agrees because 1 million is lot better than 0 million. Company B takes the bond, and sues Puerto Greco demanding the full 10 million. Even if Puerto Greco only ever pays up 2 million, Company B is still in profit. A similar thing happens with private debt. You might buy something on installments and never pay. Eventually the company you owe the money to gets tired of chasing you and sells the debt to another company cheaply. That company then chases you aggressively for the debt in the hope that you'll at least pay them something, and they can make some profit.," "Think of them as financial collection agencies. If you painted some guy's how, and they stiff you, you could try to go after the money. But you aren't very good at that, you would expend a lot of effort to maybe get 10 cents on the dollar. Or, you could sell that debt to a collection agency for 20 cents on the dollar. They are really good at chasing people down, and if they get 30 cents on dollar out of the deadbeat, that's profit. Vulture investors are the same way. An ordinary investor doesn't have the knowledge or resources to extract money for a bankrupt government. They sell that debt to someone who can do a better job at it than they can.,Think of the country like a business. article: For the purpose of this post, I am defining "capitalism" as a relatively free market system, with private ownership of the means of production. "Socialism" is defined as a system in which the means of production are owned or controlled by the state or the community as a whole, and the distribution of goods and services is controlled by the government. One potential advantage of capitalism is that it allows for innovation and competition. When businesses are free to compete with one another, they are incentivized to develop new and improved products and services, as well as new and improved methods of production. This can lead to economic growth and increased productivity. Another advantage of capitalism is that it allows individuals to pursue their own interests and goals. By allowing individuals to own and operate their own businesses, capitalism provides opportunities for people to create their own livelihoods and build their own wealth. However, one potential disadvantage of capitalism is that it can lead to income inequality. In a capitalist system, those who are successful or fortunate may accumulate a significant amount of wealth, while others may struggle to make ends meet. Additionally, without government intervention, certain industries, such as healthcare or education, may become inaccessible for those who cannot afford them. On the other hand, socialism can lead to greater equality and more universal access to resources, due to the government's ability to allocate resources and regulate industries. However, the downside of socialism is that it can stifle innovation and creativity, as government control over the means of production can limit entrepreneurial freedoms and incentives to take risks.

If taunted into the sun, they said, the Deep Woods Dragon could be defeated by the least trained of knights. The Deep Woods Dragon needed to be blinded, they said, or it would burn its attackers to ashes with rainbow-hued flames. He knew these rumors because the butterflies had told him. They were drawn to the rainbow of greens, yellows, pinks and purples of his scales, like the flowers they coveted so much. They had told him this, too, but the Dragon did not mind. The butterflies were honest, as their lives were short and beautiful. Even still, they could fly unhindered among the humans, even admired by the small humans who chased them, laughing. They told him stories while they rested on his wingtips, tail, and snout. Butterflies did not fear the Dragon, because they knew the truth. With a yawn, the Dragon shifted its weight to better perch itself on the tree's stout branch. This tree was taller than the others, and overlooked a small, circular clearing. Without the deer, the weeds thrived, covering the dirt in a green, tangled mass. At the edge of the clearing stood a massive cave entrance, vines draped over the sides of smooth rock. The Dragon had snapped off the vines in front of the entrance, to give the illusion of occupancy. This was, after all, where the humans thought he lived. He knew these rumors because the butterflies had told him. " In an ancient cave in the middle of the wood, lives an ancient dragon who's up to no good! " That was what the small humans like to chant as they chased the butterflies and laughed. So the Dragon tore at the vines, and scared the graceful deer from the peaceful clearing. He had enjoyed watching the deer with their young as they grazed the clearing. From up above in his favorite tree, they could not see him, and they could not fear him. Three times a day, the Dragon glided down from his tree to the old cave's opening. There, he took a deep breath and screamed as loud as he could. He cried in both low tones and high pitches. He wailed in imitation of female humans, shouted in a voice mimicking angry male humans. The Dragon stood on top of the cave and breathed eye-searing beams of light from his mouth to the sky. It scared the birds huddled in the trees, and the noises scared the deer far from the clearing. But they also scared the humans away from the Deep Woods. He knew these rumors because the butterflies had told him. So he made his noises, made the lights, and scared the humans away. Because any humans who saw the Dragon would discover the truth. Because, when the Dragon stepped into the sunlight, they'd see how small he really was.
