Chattering away in urgent unfamiliar tones, they had dragged me from the sea's lapping waves, tentatively tapping my face to check I was still alive. As a journalist, entry to North Korea is forbidden. Try as I might, and with the full weight of two top media agencies, there was no way I would be able pass through its gates by land or air. My editors had given up quickly - after all, it was my idea. I wanted, needed, to bag the story of 2015. How the real people of North Korea live. And if I won a prize in the meantime it wouldn't hurt the CV. A sea gypsy's boat, if you could call it that, had taken me as far as it could, but I was still miles from shore. I underestimated the tide on the approach and ended up trapped in a sandbank. I had no choice but to call for help, blowing my plan to stealthily trek the hundreds of miles to where the atrocities happened. I'd lost my camera. My phone was sitting on the sea bed. My editors had refused me the chance to take leave from work, so I told them I was headed to a writer's retreat. A digital detox. They wouldn't even begin to know where to look. As I contemplated my fate, my mind swamped with memories of survivors' stores. Mothers ripped from their children's arms. Fathers forced to choose which son to murder. Perhaps I would be a bargaining tool. More than likely, I'd be made an example of. I tried to fight against the men, who'd surrounded me and were dragging me viscously to my feet. As a pint-sized woman and as much as I loved a workout, the years of manual labour these farmers were forced to endure had given them unmovable strength. "You," I said, loudly, with as much authority as I could muster in my voice. The men stopped. "You. You want money?" They glanced at each other. "I, me, have money. Lots." I held my hands up, slowly reaching for my waterproof clip-on wallet. I pulled out more money than these people would earn in a decade and threw it over. "Take." I smiled, trying to remain unthreatening. They had power now, but money rules the world. "Dear woman, what are you doing?" I jumped, taken aback at those words. The man, the wizened old farmer, spoke in English. Perfect English. "I'm sorry, I didn't..." "Oh," the other chimed in, a smile greeting his lips as he gathered the money strewn on the floor. "Oh she's AMERICAN. One of those. Makes sense lads." "Let's take her to get freshened up. She'll want to meet the other journos who thought they'd sneak in to'hell' to get their story!" The men laughed playfully, and pity hung over their faces as they saw my hands start to tremble. We walked along a dirt track, my muscles aching from the battle to stay afloat in the brutal sea. I had to know. Needed to know. "You understand English." It wasn't a question. I tried to ensure my voice remained strong, but it wobbled. I coughed and sea water spilled from my mouth searing my throat. The man who'd been first to reveal his English accent spoke again, handing me a freshly pressed handkerchief. "Yes dear. We do. It's taught in all our schools. We learn from a young age how to articulate and enunciate in our mother tongue, as well as an array of other languages. Mandarin, Tagalog, French..." Schools? I stopped walking. "You, you go to school?" "Well, not by your standards, which are on a par with Amazonian tribes I'd say!" The men all laughed. Their scathing tones burned my ears, and a mixture of rage and fear bubbled in me. "Our schools are more like your rich countrymen's offerings. They are private. We go to school, learn languages, maths, the sciences, art... everything and anything you could wish to turn your hand to." The second farmer held my elbow as we carried on walking the path. "You see, he said, gently, "We love our country, and our Dear Leader." "How can you love that man? That murderer! He walks around like a god on earth while his people - you! - starve!" Standing in front of the men, blocking their path, I saw their faces change. Insulting their god-king would be what killed me. "HIM?" The third man spoke, before they all broke out laughing. "Oh isn't it wonderful doing this?" the first farmer said to his friends. "That god-king, as you so incorrectly call him, is our ruse. He's what takes your attention. He's our trickster, and you are our mark." I shook my head. "No," I said. "No. The reports, from your people who escape your camps. You fear him." As we reached the end of the gravel path, the men remained silent. The stones turned to asphalt, and sitting obscured by leafy green trees was a brand new car. Not a cart powered by wood or a collection of ramshackle bikes. A car. Shiny and clean. The men stopped. Two entered the sedan. The first man leaned up against it as he stretched his arms above his head, resting them folded on his chest. "Your nation, all nations of the world. They are dirty." He shuffled on his feet, getting more comfortable. "Imagine your friend and you both have a prized vase each. It had taken centuries to create, and was now yours." I looked at him, as tears graced his eyes. "Your friend. He's not clever. He doesn't appreciate it's value. He let's everyone see it, touch it. His friends don't see the value, so they crack it. Before long the porcelain is stained, the vase is damaged and it can never be what it was. It can be fixed, but the cracks will always be its weakness. That, that is the world and every land in it." I heard the trill of a mobile phone, and one of the men in the car answered, speaking Korean. "So we're all broken?" I asked. "Yes. The wars and violence, your lack of care for the weak and elderly. The orphans abandoned by your state and the widows forced out of homes. You weaken your people from birth, brainwashing them into believing material goods are success." I snorted. "So this is paradise, right?" "The vase. After seeing what your friend did to it, you decide to keeps yours safe. So when the same friends say they want to play with it, you say it's already broken. They will pester you, and laugh at you for being weak. But they will leave it alone. "Our scientists have cured diseases your people know nothing about. Our students learn skills to ensure they are entertained without the need for your internet. Our old and infirm are housed in complexes to rival palaces! "If we told the world we could cure cancer with a simple injection, you would take, and your leaders would destroy it. Because you place value on money. Your tourists would destroy our land, our people would be forced out of their homes for hotels. We place value on our people." I stood there rigidly, not wanting to believe those words. He opened the door to the car and I took a seat. We drove through towns and villages, passing houses as beautiful as Spanish villas and French chateaux. I spoke up. "All we believe. The poverty and oppression..." "We place value on our people. When tourists visit, they are shown what we want them to be shown. We have a fool parade around with your celebrities. We turn our nation's lights off at night to avoid being seen. The escapees volunteer to leave, knowing they will never see their families again. Knowing they will eventually die alone, as so many of your elderly have done." He looked glassy eyed into the distance. "They are the true casualties of this game." We arrived at a camp, nothing like what I had come to imagine I'd find. "Your people will be told you are dead. Your family can only come here if we stage a kidnapping. article: I'm a current nursing student, and while having a discussion about where nursing was going, one of my friends made the comment that nursing was only a trade and not a profession. I didn't want to believe him but after thinking about it, I think he's correct; biased on the following two factors. 1) There's nothing that nurses are allowed to do without existing orders that isn't also in the scope of practice of a CNA. 2) In order to be considered a profession you need a list of qualifications, the primary one violated by nursing is autonomy. (That is; the ability to make decisions about what and how you'll do your job.) If you can solve either of these you'll probably be able to CMV Suggested reading: I do think nurses are getting closer to becoming a profession, I just don't thing theywe are there yet. I will concede that nurses do make decisions about pt care that does directly affects outcomes, but they aren't allowed to do anything additional under their licence without the approval of an physician. Choosing not to do something that was ordered isn't autonomy. I do not lump Advanced practicing nurses in the title of trade because while they do need a physician to sign off on most of what they do, they get to make the decision about what they will do. Other factors to being a profession that I shamefully ripped straight from Wikipedia. the establishment of a training school the establishment of a university school the establishment of a local association the establishment of a national association the introduction of codes of professional ethics the establishment of state licensing laws Full disclosure: This idea sparked from a thread in TodayILearned

article: Let me preface this by saying that I am not very familiar at all with feminist positions on things. Most of my exposure to feminism has come from a few feminist acquaintances and random stuff I've seen on the internet. I'm well aware that my sampling of feminist thought is probably not representative of most feminists. With that said: I have often heard it said that the major factors in the incidence of rape are something along these lines: The media portrays women as sexualized objects, thus discouraging boys and young men from seeing women as fully human. This leads men to think that it is okay for them to rape women. We do not teach our males what consent is. Alternatively, we don't teach them that it is not okay to rape women. Now, I don't think that the first reason is a totally invalid point. I agree that the media sexualizes women to an obscene degree, and I'm sure that that has deleterious effects on the psyche of both males an females. The second point seems totally absurd to me, though. I believe that rapists know that what they're doing is wrong, but they choose to do it anyway. This goes for all kinds of rape, too. I think that both the violent rapist and the frat guy who pressures a girl into getting wasted at a party and then has sex with her while she's semi-unconscious know that what they're doing is wrong. Rather than these two points, I think that the main contributing factors to rape are psychological issues that occur as a result of trauma in childhood. I don't have any statistics to back this up, so please lambast me if this is wrong: I believe that the majority of rape victims were the victim of some sort of major abuse in childhood, most likely sexual. I also believe that the same goes for the perpetrators of abuse. People who were abused in childhood almost always reflect the repercussions of their abuse in their demeanor, and abusers can sense that. I'm not talking about anything magical, either. In my experience, victims of abuse carry themselves differently and can have personality traits that indicate that they were abused. Abusers recognize that and seek those people out as victims. In summary, I think that the main contributing factor in the incidence of rape is childhood abuse of both future victim and perpetrator. I believe that dehumanization of women through sexualization in media is a much smaller factor, and that media influence alone cannot take a boy who grew up in a healthy and supportive family and turn him into a rapist. I think that if media does have any significant effect in the incidence of rape, it is only because it reinforces the already sick foundation of someone who was abused.

article: "I'm sorry, who is this again?" The series of texts I received from the unfamiliar number read like a weird, condensed sci fi romance novel. Professions of an undying attraction - so powerful as to destroy a stellar empire - don't generally appear out of the woodwork when you're a middle-aged shut-in making their living by writing fake product reviews on the internet. "lol, it's me. Katie. From Craigslist, like..... 3 years ago? Already? Anyway, don't you remember Halloween?" I vaguely remembered being at a bar and waiting for a costume contest to begin. I had gone with a girl I'd just met; in an attempt to calm my nerves I'd been drinking, but I managed to overshoot suave and relaxed and land squarely into "WOO! DRUNK ON HALLOWEEN!" inebriation. I became the grotesque, toothy monster I was dressed as; I hobbled awkwardly around the bar, much to the amusement of the attendees and the obvious disdain of my date. You have to work the crowd if you want to win the contest, but what would SHE know about Halloween..... she didn't even wear a costume. Blasphemy. 45 minutes later I was the proud winner of a 200 bar tab. My date was nowhere to be found. I was dragged from the memory by the notification of another text: "So yeah, sorry you haven't heard from me. As I explained, things have been kind of hectic. I totally didn't mean to bail and would love to pick up where we left off!" I smiled a bit, dedicating to a two-part response: "Yes! I remember you! With the fluid dynamics degree, Subway fondness, and intense exercise routine! I just figured that the combination of my drunken jackassery and contest enthusiasm put you off..." " ..... And in a way I wish it had. You didn't dress up for Halloween - being that caliber of party pooper is a deal-breaker in my book. I appreciate the elaborate story you constructed, but I'm not interested." Over the next few minutes my phone beeped plaintively a few more times, begging me to pay attention. article: Playing football, like any other profession, is a job that one has the option of doing. No professional football player was ever forced into playing the sport. Football players in the 60's and 70's would often have to work part time jobs to support themselves and their families, some football players even giving up the sport because it was not a viable financial option. You would have to fairly uneducated to not understand that, in football, you could potentially suffer life-altering injuries. Ever person in life assesses the risks versus the rewards of their chosen profession. We all choose are professions, hence freedom of choice, and understand the risks associated. For instance, a police officer chooses his profession because of the benefits or rewards of bettering their community, but also understand the risks that they could be shot. The same can be said for firemen and those who join the army. You can say the same for today's football players. A good majority of NFL football players have obtained degrees in universities across America YET they have chosen to accept the risks involved playing football. The allure of playing in the NFL, it's benefits, and financial awards is what attracts so many potential athletes to the sport despite the potential for a life altering injury. The NFL is trying to make the game more "safe" by encouraging less violent or unnecessary hits. This has taken a lot of out of the game. We are caging some of the NFL's best athletes by employing some of these safeguards. Even NFL players...the ones who accept this physical punishment do not agree with these safeguards and believe that these rules are hurting the game. article: There are 3 ways to put out a fire. 1- Remove oxygen, 2- Remove heat, 3-remove fuel. We can't remove oxygen from the atmosphere so that's out. To cool it down you can spray water but that isn't feasible for the length of the fire. You can hit small sections with air tankers, helicopters or fire trucks but it is only for high value areas like houses. You don't have enough water, pumps and hoses to spray down every inch, so the main option is to remove fuel. How? Bulldozers or crews with chainsaws and hand tools create a fire break. You can clear brush and dig a fire break down to about 3 feet wide and 6" deep to the dirt clear out the dead leaves, grass, roots, etc that will burn. That way the fire burns until it hits the line and has nothing left to burn, and it puts itself out. You can also create a smaller, more controlled fire to burn up all the fuel before the fire burns it in an out of control manner, but that is where the phrase "back fire" comes from. But if the wind carries burning embers or a tree falls across the fire line the fire will escape and continue to spread. If there is a strong wind it is too dangerous to dig line and it easily crosses the line you already built. That is why you rely on rain, calm winds and cooler weather to help, because there simply isn't enough resources to possibly stop a raging fire on our own.','A combination of rural and semi-rural areas which are far from main roads, or easy sources of water. Strong winds (called Santa Ana winds) which accelerates the spread of the fire. Lots of dry grasses and bushes from regular rapid growthdrying cycles.

article: I honestly don't understand why many point out what a "failure" Occupy was as a protest. I believe that: 1) The mainstream media was a huge driving force for convincing the public that it had no direction or purpose. I think this is intentional, as it's touted as a failure to dissuade the public from trying something like it again. Downplaying it is their attempt at quelling the masses. I believe that Occupy WAS significant because it 2) created a global outpouring of support, galvanizing hundreds of thousands (perhaps millions?) of people all over the world onto the streets. Though we look with envy to Turkey and Brazil at their ability to stand up and cite how we Americans are lazy, we started Occupy! 3) brought together people from all walks of life for a number of different, yet still related causes. While some claim that it was detrimental that there seemed to be no single cause of protest, the same thing is going on in Brazilthey're protesting not just bus fares, but so many other things from corruption to crony capitalism. 4) highlighted innovative solutions to problems, like the communications system of having entire groups relay messages in unison to overcome loudspeaker rules. 5) brought to light ideas and concepts not often discussed: the barter system, direct democracy, alternative currencies, buying local, the failed two party system... though these haven't yet sprouted, Occupy helped plant these seeds into our collective psyche as to their possibilities. I think the "solutions" aspect of the protest goes largely ignored, but was one of the most powerful parts of the movement. 6) we better understand what we're up against: before, it was considered absurd to think that the police would attempt to co-opt and infiltrate peaceful protests, or that they'd use violence to such a degree. While this was a painful lesson, I think it helped us wise up to the nature of the government. While their tactics may cause some to believe protests are ineffective, others see it as all the more reason why we NEED to be protesting. I like having my views changed and picked apart. So here you go. Now, why do you think Occupy was a failure? Are there any lessons to learn, or should it be tossed like an old carcass from our memories, not worthy of resuscitation? EDIT: It's midnight here so I'm going to bed. Apologies if statements of mine were unclear. I've somewhat changed my view in that 1) Occupy should have had more tangible results for a protest of its size, and 2) Yes, their over-ambition to implement lofty solutions got the best of them. I'm still really optimistic that the movement could lead to other protests that have learned from its mistakes. I still think the problems of society raised by Occupy are exceptionally valid and in dire need of reform. HOW this will be done on a large scale by the masses... well, not sure. If no such change is forthcoming, then I would view Occupy as an abysmal failure.

article: While [videos like this] can easily explain exactly how an unofficial two party system forms from a fist past the post electoral system, it is often heavily implied that this is a self-evidently bad thing. In my opinion, that belief is based on a few very naive understandings of politics: 1. People blaming every perceived troublesome aspect that they witness in politics in general, on their particular system as a scapegoat, from partisanship, to gridlocks, and "corruption," without any thought put into exactly how a many-party system would stop these, or even looking at evidence to see whether these problems are indeed lower in the proportional voting systems of Europe. 2. The belief in an idealized dream of a progressive and pure outsider "Third Party," that just happens to represent everything that the speaker stands for, rather than various new shades of the same basic left wing and right wing ideologies, half of which will need to form a coalitional government together anyways, and become a closed system. 3. The glorification of the congressparliament as the ultimate representation of the people's will. In reality, democracy is the tool through which millions of different opinions can be channeled into a single majority that can govern. Primary elections inside a party, and tactical voting for the big party that you hate the least can be elements of this, as much as throwing a dozen different parties into the parliament and letting them organize such a single government there. At the same time, obvious disadventages of many-party systems are ignored: 1. The need for a coalition if there is no party reaching an absolute majority, means that a smaller party can get into not just parliament, but into government itself, if a deal is made between party leaders through backdoor politics, regardless of whether the majority of their individual voters would have supported such a coalition. 2. This can cause not just idealistic reformer parties, but also extremists getting into authority, which can eventually lead to a dictatorship. Contrast with moderate two party system that might be neither quick to reform, but nor to radicalism. 3. Proportionally distributing the votes among representatives means that people are voting for party lists, not just for rivalous local representatives. This takes away the possibility of representatives fine-tuning their platform to local interests, and makes it necessary for them to vote along party lines.

article: I sit in the cafe sipping my hot chocolate calmly. My entire body aches from running for so long. I look to the window keeping alert. I would have to leave soon and head to the train station; Charlie was the smartest cop that I knew and in all likelihood he was already on my trail. I throw out the cup and grab my backpack ready to go. I look at the train time schedule once I get to the station and deliberate my destination. The secret to being on the run was never having a set plan. If I didn't know where I was going, neither would anyone else. I decide to head upstate towards the countryside; although farming communities were often tightly knit, there were fewer cops and they seemed to be less suspicious than those in the city. I sit on the train and read a magazine. I sense someone sit next to me but I'm too tired to care. I imagine a cozy queen sized bed with tons of pillows that I have to just myself and yawn. The person next to me chuckles and exclaims, " Crime is tiring, huh? " I look up worriedly to see Charlie sitting next to me. He snaps a set of handcuffs one on my wrist and one on the seat. I look around fearfully and he laughs. " There is no one here. I'm not even on duty. We'll get off at the first stop and I'll call in some back up, " he says in an amused tone. I roll my eyes, " Please Charlie, you have to let me go, " I plead. He looks at me disgusted, " You are a murderer, you deserve to be punished, " he says. I shake my head frustrated; I couldn't tell him the truth because he would never believe it. I imagine my " victim's " face. She has short black hair and rosy cheeks, I'm sure she was happy wherever she was. She was only nineteen when she murdered Charlie. After his death, I received a small button in the mail which said, " Press to go back in time ." I pressed it and when she was born, I stole her from the hospital and I left her at a random police station in South Carolina. I figured that she would be put in the foster care system and adopted. I hoped she'd have a better chance with new parents and at the very least I figured that dropping her off so far away would protect Charlie. I couldn't tell anyone or she would be tracked down and returned to her parents doomed to make the same mistakes. Everyone assumed I murdered the baby because she was still missing after all this time and while it sucked, the first time losing Charlie was painful enough; I wasn't going to let it happen again. I look at Charlie and then close my eyes; I was tired of running. " Why did you do it? " he asks quietly. I laugh and answer, " She's not dead. She's just adopted. " He was never going to believe a word out of my mouth. The News had painted me as a maniacal baby killer and my story wasn't exactly the most rational. " Where is she? " he asks picking up my backpack and beginning to go through it. I blush wondering what he'll pull out. I shake my head, " It doesn't matter, " I reply as he pulls out my scrapbook. ' Well this was going to be interesting'I think as he begins to flip through the pages. He wears a puzzled face and says, " You look very nice in these wedding pictures, what happened to your husband? " I smile; of course Charlie would see a picture of himself and think it was someone else. " He died, " I say quietly looking at Charlie's young inquisitive face focused on my scrapbook. He closes the book and puts it back in my bag, " I'm sorry for your loss. Hopefully you'll be able to plead insanity or land in an institution where you can get proper help to cope. " I begin to feel tears in my eyes and look at the handcuff, " Can I go to the bathroom? " I ask. Charlie shakes his head and replies, " Nope. " He was a good cop and wasn't easily fooled. Escaping in the bathroom would be a disgrace for him; I don't think he'd ever forgive himself for that mistake. I wipe my eyes with my free hand and he hands me a tissue. Even when dealing with what he believed was a murderer, he was never cruel. I begin to hyperventilate with worry and he looks at me concerned. " Take a deep breath and just relax. Everything is going to be okay, " he says softly. Charlie had anxiety too and sympathized with anyone who suffered through it as well. I cough and try to distract myself by thinking of good memories. " Can I tie up my hair? " I ask quietly as my tears act as glue between my hair and my face. He looks at me suspiciously and sighs before tying up my hair himself. I chuckle, " You must hate me, " I say. He shakes his head and replies, " You're just sick. You're not evil. " He unlocks the handcuff and grabs my arm tightly. He escorts me off the train and we head to the front of the station. He calls for back up on his cell phone and they arrive within fifteen minutes. A rookie officer puts me in real handcuffs and reads me my rights before leading me to his squad car. I get the feeling that he is very new to the squad from how loose the handcuffs are. I lean against the car tiredly and I hear, " Officer Wilds! " The rookie looks at me curiously and tells me to wait before running over to the older officer. I look around and see that Charlie is being interviewed by two other officers and a lieutenant talking to the rookie. I walk to the front of the car and slip out of the extremely loose handcuffs. I grab my backpack and slip away into an alley way with a smile. I was still tired but at least I wouldn't be sleeping in a cell.

article: I clambered through the woods, twigs snapping and leaves rustling under my feet - the deeper I got the darker it got, and the darker it got the more I tripped and slipped until one moment I was running and then next I was floored. I could hardly tell what had happened. I lifted my face and fell again, unable to straighten the inside of my head and process a single thought. I wiped the mud from my face and turned helplessly, still on the ground. My pursuers, those creatures, were gone. I moved over, transitioning from a climb to a stumble to a walk to a jog to a run. I stopped. Their bodies lay there, broken and raked. I felt a warm air behind me and turned to see a face. Not the face of a person, the face of a beast. The darkness was gone - it was just a forest. The creature eyed me suspiciously, and then moved backwards to give me space. "I missed one? Hmm..." The voice was deep and gravelly. The dragon seemed ancient. I froze as it leaned upwards and spread it's wings proudly, looking down on me. I was beyond running away. I was too shocked to even move. "I have slept in these woods for five thousand years - six? - and this is the first time in all of those years that one of the itty bitties has seen me. How curious. Though I should think you have things to be more afraid of than some dark and sounds, hm?" I didn't speak. "Yes, indeed. Six thousand years asleep and I intend to sleep for six thousand more. You can not be allowed the chance to share this information. I am terribly sorry it has to end like this, but one itty bitty life is a small price to pay for my thousands of years." "You haven't done anything in six thousand years." I couldn't believe I was speaking. "You won't do anything for six thousand more. Any human life is worth more than that." I backed up. "Oh?" The dragon seemed a little perplexed, but then appeared to ponder the remark. "That is an interesting sentiment, little itty bitty. Walk with me." And so I followed the dragon through the woods. It seemed so peaceful now. Rays of sunshine shone through the leaves of the green trees, and we walked down a neat little pathway. "I remember the first human I had to kill. Just before I went to sleep. Dragonslayers, they were. Heroes, they thought themselves. My brothers and sisters were a little more aggressive than I. None of them live today." The sorrow in his voice was evident." We came to a clearing, with a pool. The dragon sat in this pool. "One day such a'hero' came to my woods. That is when I killed him. He attacked me and I failed. I was distraught. It was that day I decided to sleep. As the last dragon I carry the burden of all those before me, and I would not allow myself to do what my siblings had done. So I restrained myself. I slept. But they kept coming. I had to kill many to stay hidden. I would not kill the masses when they came for me. I would never let them know my hiding place." The creature was tired. I saw squirrels and butterflies. I saw flowers blooming out of nowhere. The whole place became so peaceful, yet..... The dragon was tired. "I eventually desensitivised myself to that killing, I suppose. I had to wait until the tales of the dragons became myth. You are the first in six thousand years." I swallowed. I didn't even speak. "Itty bitty..." " ..... You've hardly even spoken, yet you've taught me so much. Perhaps this is not my place in this world. To hide away from the world to protect it, only to destroy whatever gets too close..." I was confused. I didn't understand what I had taught this dragon. The sunshine grew more intense. "These woods have been lost to the dark for so long. I can not count how many heroes with good intentions died at my claw. I wonder if I can save more." The dragon stood, extended its wings, and ascended. The woods didn't change again. They were still green. The greenest woods I've ever known. It took me a night's rest to truly understand what I had witnessed. To this day I live alone, in a little log cabin. A little log cabin in a clearing, next to a pool, in the greenest woods I've ever known. I will not soon forget what happened when I first saw this place. Sometimes I think I hear a great sound of beating wings. But whenever I look, I never see a thing. - It's so damn easy to tell a BookWyrm writing prompt just by reading the title.:

article: Often I've heard people who have no problem abusing alcohol or marijuana rationalizing their habits by saying they don't do "hard" drugs. Because heroin, meth, and crack are avoided, abusing other drugs is easier to justify. This is symptomatic of drug education that fails to differentiate between use and abuse, and instead differentiates between good drugs and bad drugs. Alcohol and nicotine are legal, and excessive drinking or smoking are is not as big of a problem as just one experience with a "bad" drug. An environment that prioritizes which specific drug is being used over how said drug is being used makes it difficult for young people to learn how to manage drugs, whether it's tylenol or crack cocaine. I've seen alcohol be as "hard" of a drug as anything out there, and put people in unsettling, unsafe, and terrifying situations. I've also seen alcohol turn people cheerful and docile. The fact of the matter is, different drugs affect different people differently. The separation of "hard" drugs and "soft" drugs ignores this, and lazily tries to skirt the education and information aspect of responsible drug use. I would not take or recommend that anyone take heroin or meth. In my experience these drugs are veritable life-ruiners that really do fuck people up. However, I still treat any drug with the same respect that I would a bag of black tar. Drugs aren't sentient beings dedicated to destroying life, but they are powerful, powerful substances whether one considers them "hard" or not. CMV please! Hello, users of CMV! article: My old bones creaked as long disused muscles hauled me up the cold mountain road. It's been sixteen years since the floodwaters released my coffin from my grave, since my eyes burned at the first light in countless decades. My mind had long since lost language and misplaced memories. The dark will do that to you. The first few days, or months maybe, I had passed the time remembering the songs from my village tavern, the stories from my family's past, and the lovely girls who no doubt awaited my return. I expected my family to release me any moment, as soon as the cemetery sexton could be bought off. Days turned to months, and I felt the ground grow cold around me. I don't remember giving up. I didn't care at first, I knew I could pop up in another village a few hundred miles away, build a life, and forget the circumstance of my unfortunate disposition. As my waiting grew longer I grew more angry at the bastards who put me in that hole. They knew what they did to me. I don't remember going mad. But surely I did. And then nothing. Nothing until I felt my coffin sliding, and breaking up, and water filling my mouth and nose and lungs. I washed up on the shore, no idea who or where or why I was. Months later and with the kindness of strangers, I started to think again. In time, slowly, my memories returned, in little snippets at first. Confusion as my new language clashed with the tongue of my memories. And then, hatred. Anger. A desire for revenge. It took me four years to piece together enough memories to fully understand what happened to me. I was a John Smith, an unknown, a medical marvel with amnesia. Once I understood what my memories meant, I couldn't share them any more. In time, I researched my family, finding old baptismal records and death records. My death record. The records of my village and my people. I walked on, leaning heavily on my walking staff, years of nutrition and life not having fully made up for three hundred years of waiting. I passed the loch where my family watered their animals, and found the outline of a foundation, and then another. I turned to face the bastards, the men who sent me to my hell. Four weathered stones marked their final resting places. I spit on their graves, and finally my walking staff could no longer hold me up against the pull of the ground. I wept, cursing their names as I felt the futile anger burn. I can have no revenge. The plague, the only thing that could take any like us from this life, took them. And left me.

If it does happen in front of the jury, the judge tells the jury to ignore it (and, IIRC, will often quickly explain why to ignore it). If it seriously compromises the integrity of the trial, the judge can declare a mistrial (meaning that this trial got screwed up and can't be fixed, so you start over with a new jury). article: What is polygamy. I realize that polygamy can be a woman with multiple husbands, or several people in a same-sex relationship. By definition, it doesn't have to be a man with multiple wives. In theory it could be any combination of genders of three or more people. However, in reality, the vast majority of polygamous relationships tend to be multiple female partners per male partner. So it seems silly to pretend that it's going to be anything else. Polygamy and same-sex marriage are dissimilar. A lot of people like to argue "if gay marriage can be legalized, then why not polygamy?" I've heard this both from opponents to same-sex marriage, and from people who support polygamy. It doesn't make any sense from either source. The only thing that same-sex marriage and polygamy have in common is that they're both (a) types of relationships and (b) currently illegal (although, less so for same-sex marriage.) They have the same minimal similarities that interracial marriage and adult-child marriages had in the 1960's. It doesn't logically follow that, since we legalized interracial marriage, we have to legalize adult-child marriages. And similarly, it doesn't logically follow that if we legalize same-sex marriage that we need to legalize polygamy. Keeping same-sex marriage illegal has higher costs than keeping polygamy illegal. If you're gay, and same-sex marriage is illegal, then you have two choices; either remain unmarried or marry someone to which you have no attraction. Both are pretty dismal options. Contrast this with if you're a straight, married man and wish to take on another wife. The fact that polygamy is illegal, means that you can't, but the situation that it pushes you into isn't that bad, because you still have the legal right to be married to your wife. So you can still be married to the kind of person you want, just not as many people as you like. Where-as, with same sex marriage being illegal, then you can't even get married to the kind of person you want. Harms of polygamy There are two main harms I see with polygamy; one symbolic and the other more concrete. The first is that it creates a relationship where a man gets multiple women but each woman gets a fraction of a man. In that sense it implicitly supports the idea that a man is multiple times as valuable as a woman, but each woman is a fraction as valuable as a man. Further, it creates unequal power within the relationship. While the man no longer has to compete, each woman still has to compete both with other women within the relationship and other possible partners outside the relationship. The second problem is that it's completely unsustainable. There simply aren't enough women, relative to men, for men to have more than one partner on average. And if you try to get around this, it leads to some very unsavory situations. Consider this; a polygamous society in which each man has 1.2 wives on average. (So, not even everyone is in a polygamous relationship, and those that are don't even have a huge number of wives). In each generation, there are roughly equal number of men and women born. So, for the first generation of polygamous men to have 1.2 wives, they would need to marry all the women in their own generation and 20 of the women in the next generation. For the second generation, there will only be 8 single women for each single man. So, just to have one wife each, the men in the second generation will marry all the remaining women in their own generation, plus 20 of the next generation. And to have 1.2 wives each, they will marry an additional 20 of the next generation. For the third generation of men to have 1.2 wives each, they will need to marry all their remaining female cohorts plus 60 of the next generation. This continues on and on until there's a generation of men that have to marry completely from the generation below them. And then dip into two generations below them, etc. A lot of the most infamous polygamous societies (like the FLDS) end up having adult men married to young girls. This isn't a coincidence. Polygamy, as an institution, can only be supported by marrying younger and younger women. Or by ejecting men from their society. This is another problem that you commonly see in real life polyamous communities; often only one son from each family will be allowed to stay, and all the rest will just be kicked out of the community when they turn 18. This is the only way they can maintain a gender imbalance. This is both incredibly cruel to the young men who are abandoned by their families and communities, and it is damaging to society at large. It doesn't fix the "excess" of men, as much as just moving it out of the polygamous community and into society at large, where it is more diluted. In summary, Polygamy has almost nothing in common with same-sex marriage. Having it illegal has much smaller costs, and legalizing it has far greater harms. For all these reasons, I believe that comparing them is ridiculous and that it should remain illegal. CMV.

article: So, it seems like your question is "could I make a fake wire transfer from a non-existent financial institution to a real one?" I've worked in the AML side of financial compliance and the short answer is: because the recipient bank would not accept the money as real. Banks (and other financial institutions) know each other and all have sophisticated transaction monitoring set-ups. Your wire from a bank which doesn't exist with a bunch of identifying characteristics which don't exist (there's a lot of embedded data in this kind of transfer), would be flagged not just because it's large but because they can't confirm the provenance of the money. If your idea is to start a fake bank, you'll run into a bigger problem with a whole bunch of regulatory authorities. Especially in order to get to where the largest and most established institutions are: the presumption that money coming from them is good money. There's a decent amount of trust that goes into "if BofA says this money exists we'll take as a given that it does," and it requires having been a well-established institutions. So now you've started a bank, it's twenty years in and you have all of that trust and confidence, are in compliance, and have customers. Would you really throw all of that away plus risk jail time to fraudulently get maybe a million dollars?

article: uvtcabbage is correct, but I'll expand on that by explaining the [bomb calorimeter] (URL0). This is a device where you place a given mass of food eg 100 grams, and combust it completely in the presence of excess oxygen in a sealed container known as a bomb. The heat released from the combustion reaction is absorbed by water surrounding the bomb and the resulting temperature rise is recorded with a thermometer. The heat of combustion (in calories or joules) can then be calculated using the mass of the food and the temperature rise of the water. This process is known as bomb calorimetry and is used to determine the caloric content of foods, which can be used to estimate the amount of energy a person can obtain from consuming them.

article: The rain from the thunderstorm outside lashed against the train as I strode down the aisle, dripping from the deluge outside. There'd been delays all morning, and this train was unusually crowded as a result. Every seat seemed to be occupied, the cars packed with humans in various states of bedragglement. I had just about given up hope, resigning myself to standing, when I noticed an empty seat at the end of the car. Gratefully, I made my way over and plonked myself down next to a brown-haired girl who couldn't have been more than ten. She looked up at me as I sat down and gave a faint but warm smile. I couldn't help returning it, thankful to finally have found a spot to take the weight off my feet. As I did, I noticed the girl's hands, resting gently on her legs. Each hand was loosely holding a cell phone. They were the same model, as far as I could tell, though I wasn't sure exactly which model it was. They looked older, like something from the early 2000s. The one in her left hand was black, while the one in her right hand was white. She followed my gaze, angling her head downward to peer at her own hands. She blinked. Then, she lifted her head again, looking right into my eyes. Now she was positively beaming. I was taken slightly aback, but I was still feeling quite pleased to have found a seat at all, and the girl's smile was infectious. I grinned back in spite of myself. "What's got you so chuffed?" I asked, in good humor. The girl continued to smile, but shook her head slightly. I looked at her for a moment, and then it was my turn to blink. The girl was still looking at me, and still grinning like a Cheshire cat. I cleared my throat, as my smile became more fixed. With a jerk that I had vainly hoped would look natural, I moved my head and began making a show of looking for the morning's paper, which I'd stashed in my briefcase. When I'd retrieved it, the girl was placidly staring out the window, watching as the water rushed down the pane in rivulets. Her hands remained in her lap, loosely holding the phones. Confused, but also somewhat relieved, I turned to the financial section to finish an article on precious metals that I'd been perusing early. When I finished, I leafed to the crossword puzzle, using the cover of turning pages to steal a glance at my tiny seatmate. She had not moved, and I found myself smiling slightly, as I wondered about this unusual child and her two cell phones. Presently, I turned my attention back to my paper and busied myself decoding a few clues. It was just a few minutes later that the train began to slow, heralding our imminent arrival. I folded my paper, reaching down for my briefcase, as the train slowed to a stop. I felt something brush against my leg and caught the flash of a brown ponytail as it weaved into the crowd, disappearing amongst my fellow commuters. Chuckling slightly, I lifted my briefcase and made to stand when something caught my eye - the girl's cellphone, the black one. I pursed my lips - I didn't really have time for this - and reached out towards the phone. It immediately started to ring, moving slightly across the seat as it vibrated. I withdrew my hand. The ringing stopped. The furrow in my brow increased and, telling myself I was being silly, I reached out again for the old phone. Again it started to ring. I hesitated. The phone was almost off the seat now, the vibration moving it steadily closer to the edge. I scooped it up and looked at it. The screen was illuminated but there was nothing to read, just an artificial blue-white glow. The ringing continued. Almost without meaning to, I pushed the green call button, and put the phone to my ear. "Hallo?" Static. A musical, tinkling laugh. Then nothing. The screen had gone dark. I held the phone in my hand, frowning down at it. Shrugging, I slipped it into my pocket and exited the train, hastening to catch the last of the stragglers moving into the station. So focused was I on my destination that I didn't see the small girl in front of me, and almost bowled her over. I skidded to a stop on the rain soaked concrete, just inches from the girl. "You gave me quite a fright," I said, half relieved, half annoyed. The girl merely smiled at me, making no move to apologize or step to the side. I blinked. Again. Coming back to myself, I plunged my hand into the pocket of my coat, drawing out the black phone. I held it out to the girl, who continued smiling impassively. "You forgot this," I said, somewhat (in my opinion) gratuitously. But the girl only smiled wider, staring into my eyes as she ignored the phone in front of her. Slowly, she shook her head. "Keep it." Her voice was deeper and richer than it should have been, aged and full-bodied. It was the voice of a woman, not the small girl standing beside me. Inadvertently, I took a step back. The girl's eyes seemed to sparkle with mischief, as her smile stretched to its largest size yet, relegating her eyes to twin twinkling slits. "Keep it," she repeated. And with a swish of her ponytail, she was gone, melting back into the crowd of the station. I stood rooted to the spot, staring at the black phone still clutched in my hand. It was warm, with a reassuring weight, and almost without thinking, I went to pocket it. I had just felt the tiny bounce as the phone came to a rest against my thigh, breaking my reverie, when I heard the barest hint of a voice float over the assembled crowd: "And next time, pick up on the first call."

A huge shockwave swept the entire radius like a storm, sweeping everything in its path with a ferocious force. The ferry tipped to its side as Charon struggled to keep it afloat, dust and debris clouding his sight. Rocks and boulders cracked from the walls, rolling into the waters with a huge crush. Loud humming of machinery reverberated from the vicinity. Line after line of huge metallic tanks drove through the huge hole created by the explosion, their turrets protruding through the choking coat of dust and debris. "Weitergehen! Keep moving!" A voice shouted from one of the armored vehicles amidst the whirring chaos. He stepped out of the vehicle in a black trenchcoat and a visored cap. He stepped into the rubble, as he strode towards the shore, his eyes darting across the river. The vehicles soon came to a stop, several doors opened as uniformed men came out of the trucks. Their shoulders strapped in rifles, as they encompassed the shorter man. He held his hands over his crotch as he surveyed the distance, a crooked smile forming under his odd moustache. "Friedrich!" He called out in an authoritarian high pitch. A man broke through the large crowd armed in guns as he rushed to his beckon, fondling a paper in his hand. "Zend out ze letter. I want you to write all ze details as I instructed earlier. I want it to reach to him in time." The moustached man posed in a stoic posture, his eyes still darting across the shore, as if in search for something. "But fuhrer, in all respect he will need some proof of this expedition. Not many men would find this believable froma sheet of paper." Friedrich replied timidly. The moustached man strode forward across the shore over the rubble, staring at the cowering souls, several crushed under the huge weight of the boulders. "What was ze name of his deceased daughter?" He asked. "Marigold Churchill. But she died in 1921, sir." Friedrich responded, his fingers busy scribbling across the paper. A smug of satisfaction wore his face again as he peered into the crowd. If his knowledge was correct, the ferrier of the dead travelled every fourty years. He turned toward the souls, clearing his voice in preparation. "If your name zis Marigold Churchill, I oblige you to step forward!" His voice echoed through the cavernous vicinity, ripples of murmurs stirred amongst the crowd. "You have nothing to fear! Some of you may recognise who I am. But I am looking for Marigold Churchill, zere zis someone she has to meet." The crowd of again replied in a murmur. A small path opened between them, as they parted way for an unknown figure to pass through. Tiny feet pitter pattered across the rubble, walking towards the voice that called out for her. He craned towards her direction. Watching her appearance as she cleared from the gathering crowd as they peered down at her. Curiosity bubbling from the questioning faces. He tried to contain the chuckle but it was all in vain. He watched as her feeble hands stretch out to his, as he stretched out his own in response. He knelt down on one knee as he gazed at the child. Her infant palms holding onto his, as they stared upon each other. "Friedrich." He called out, his eyes still lingering at upon his new found companion. "Yes, my fuhrer." He stood up as he carried the child into his arms. "Where was our next targeted destination?" He chucked as the child stroked his thick mass of moustache, fondling it in her fingers. "It was Russia, my fuhrer." Friedrich answered in a tremoulous cadence, trepidation evident in his words, fearing the response that was going to leave his master's toungue. He watched his Fuhrer's eyes, as they danced maniacally as they gazed upon the innocent child. He followed those eyes, as they changed their gaze from the child, and darted towards the Charon, who hovered in the murky waters of the Styx. "Friedrich, cancel that schedule. We have a new destination."

article: Firstly, downforce has far more to do with cornering than it does acceleration. Only in extremely high-powered vehicles is there the potential for the drive wheels to break traction at the kind of speeds where downforce-generating aero aids are effective. It's far more common for these'spoilers' to be employed to keep the vehicle stable during high speed cornering. For this reason, the comment about them being useless on front-wheel-drive vehicles is entirely incorrect. Aerodynamic aids can (and most definitely are) built into the front of vehicles to create downforce over the front wheels. Without these downforce-generating structures, the general shape of a vehicle (flat on the bottom, curved over the top) can often imitate the function of a plane's wing - the lower air pressure over the top of the vehicle causes lift to be generated at high speeds, leading to instability. Generally this is insignificant on normal road-going passenger vehicles, but high performance sports car, supercars, and race cars are often capable of speeds where it can be an issue. A related factor is weight. Normal passenger vehicles are usually noticably heavier than their sportsrace counterparts. The extra weight provides a downward force on the tyres, improving the lateral grip during cornering. As a result, no (or minimal) aero aids are needed. However, in race cars weight is considered (for the most part) undesirable as it has negative effects on acceleration and handling. So, how do you get the benefit of weight (the downward push on the tyres that increases grip) without the extra mass that creates inertia and resists changes of direction? You use air to push down on the car. The force is applied, but you aren't penalised by carrying extra mass. There's a downside to this though - more aerodynamic downforce creates more drag. Cornering improves, but top speed suffers. Booooo! Huge amounts of time and money are spent on tuning the aerodynamic properties of high performance vehicles to balance the application of downforce to improve cornering, and the minimisation of drag to maximise top speed and acceleration.," "The harder the tires are pressed down, the less they'll slide or spin, so a spoiler on a real race car helps the car stay stuck to the road. They push down on the rear of the car, so if your problem is that your drive wheels spin when you floor it, and the drive wheels are in front, pushing down on the rear won't really help.

article: I swear a lot in this one. Please don't read if you're easily offended. "What the fuck?" was the best I could muster to break the uncomfortable silence, as the wind blew behind me. "You've only ever saved yourself!" she cried from the other end of the roof. "We lost fifteen guys less than a MONTH ago and all you did was cover your sorry ass!" I took a deep breath. I know it's cliche. But it took all my strength not to flip out and send one of us off this roof on a rapid journey to the street below. "And what if I hadn't, huh? What if I hadn't covered my ass? What then?" She was silent. By now, people had begun to notice that there were two lunatics yelling at each other on a roof. In fact, if I wasn't being modest, I'd say we attracted a small crowd at street level. Some were no doubt scared I was going to jump. And, to be honest, I'd considered it. L'appel du vide. "If I hadn't'covered my sorry ass', I'd be dead. They'd know I got in. I fucked enough shit up in there that it was literally impossible to miss. And do you know what would have happened if they got me?" Again, silence. "You'd be dead. Jon would be dead. Sue, Tim, everyone on our fucking floor. Gone. Because if I can get in without having to kill one of them, they'll sure as hell get in to our shit if they did kill one of us." I turned to face away from her, and stared at the street. People were watching, but nobody really cared. All people wanted to know was whether one of us was going to jump. No attention was paid to what was actually going on. "So what if they get into your shit? You work on a five-year-old crappy Dell, and do absolutely fuck-all! The worst they'd find on there is a saved game of Minesweeper!" I snapped back around and almost marched halfway over to her. "The hell would you know about what I do all day? I have access to every system this goddamn place runs! We get hacked, we lose everything!" She gazed up at the sky. Obviously, none of this was going in. I came closer. "Look. People invest their entire life savings with this place. We have the power to ruin people's lives. We can turn people out of their houses." "You work in IT at a bank! Why the fuck did people die?" I sighed. I knew this was coming. "I fucked up." "We all know! That's why we're in this mess! But it still doesn't explain why people got killed!" "No. You think that's a fuck-up. You have no idea what I did." She ran over to me. I could see her breath in the air as she jogged. "About three months ago, that time the network went down. I got it back up and said everything was fine." "Yes..." she replied, not sure where I was going with this. "I didn't notice it at first. But I left a gaping security hole in our servers. Someone broke in. A team of people, probably." "What the fuck did you do?!" she asked, agitated. I turned away again, looked up at the sky, and shouted. "I lost thirteen billion dollars!" The silence was twice as uncomfortable as the last, and was a good ten seconds long before she spoke again. "How the fuck did that lead to deaths?" She was whispering now, obviously not wanting to be overheard. I probably shouldn't have shouted that to the heavens, with hindsight. "I don't know. I didn't think. It was an impulse; I sent people after them. I did everything I could to trace them and sent people there. How was I to know they'd be armed?" I was whispering as well. "So people died. Why did you have to cover your ass?" She was like a child listening to a grandparent tell them a story about the war, except a lot more eager. "I..... I had to get the money back," I explained, hesitantly. "I didn't know what to do. I got it from wherever I could." "I still don't understand why you couldn't have saved them as well!" She was shouting again. Probably a bad move. "I tried! I failed!" She was shaking her head. "I can only do so much. But don't you for a second think I only saved myself." "Oh yeah?" she retorted. "Who the fuck else did you save?" "We're still in business. Nobody else died. And now, nobody but you knows what I did." She stepped back in stunned silence. "I can't deal with this any more," I half-said. I'm not sure if the words actually came out of my mouth. I jogged over to the stairwell. I was just going to go back downstairs and get on with the rest of the day's work. What she would do when I didn't show up tomorrow, I don't know. EDIT: Formatting. Markdown, we are not friends.

article: I'm sorry I don't have any hard science. As the title says essentially I don't believe the automobile as we know it today serves any purpose other than getting material (human or otherwise) from point A to point B. To start off I'm just gonna go ahead and define automobile as four wheels, and engine, and an exhaust and it seats 2 people. I see automobiles as a necessary evil. They're not ideal for long term transportation (trips longer than 4 hours) as they get cramped and uncomfortable but if there aren't alternative modes of transportation to where you're headed it's a necessary evil. For short term there are different and better ways to get around. For example in a city it may be more advantageous to take a rail, bike, or walk to where you need to go. The frequent use of automobile has created this large network of pedestrian unfriendly highways and roadways through cities and countrysides. Even with the proper training there are just a percentage of accidents you're not going to be able to avoid no matter how good of a driver you are. As well as the inefficiency of how many people you can fit in a car and the frequency with which the car is used and the number of cars on the road currently has lead to many unsolvable problems that large urban cores face today. If an automobile is to be used at all, its use should be strictly utilitarian and nothing more. This is also why I detest car company ads. We've all seen the ad, where some slick camera work displays this beautiful polished car while some cool song is playing and this car is just tearing it up on open asphalt with not another soul around. The reality of the situation is that those 250 some odd horses are going to be useless when you're barely dragging your feet going 5 mph bumper to bumper on the interstate. It sickens me that there are people who drive cars for fun. I'm not a radical environmentalist but I don't honestly think that you can justify in this day and age driving a car around to cool your head or to relax. I could understand maybe if you wanted to drive TO somewhere so you can go to that place and relax, but driving just to clear your head? Ridiculous. Regarding off-roading: Unacceptable and a blatant misuse of what a vehicle should be. Regarding racing sports: This seems okay in my book. I hesitate to call it a sport because there are so many factors within a car as that could be different that I can't see it as a test of skill between drivers but more as a test of engineering between manufacturing companies. But that's a CMV for another time. Technically it falls within the definition that it takes the driver to the finish line, the goal of the sport being who can get there the fastest. Considering the large effects that cars have had in shaping our society I believe that they are a tool and nothing more. They can be a symbol of wealth much like an expensive hammer can be a symbol of wealth as opposed to a cheap plastic one. But like you would never go around smashing things senselessly with your expensive hammer, I think aimless trips in a car are ethically, financially, and functionally unjustifiable. Change my view. article: Before the Marian reforms, the Roman military forces were exclusively made up of citizens people of property (3500 sesterces, say about 1750 loaves of bread) and capable of supplying their own equipment. This meant that only a small fraction of the population was eligible to serve in the army, and those who did were typically well-trained and well-equipped. However, with the expansion of the Roman Empire and the need for larger armies, the Roman Republic faced challenges in maintaining a standing army of citizen soldiers. In response, the consul Gaius Marius introduced a series of reforms in the late 2nd century BC that opened up the Roman army to a wider pool of recruits. Under the Marian reforms, the Roman army became a professional force that was open to all free men, regardless of property qualifications. The government now supplied soldiers with their equipment and they were paid a salary, which made it easier for poorer men to enlist. The army was also reorganized into legions, each of which was composed of the same standard units and supported by a standardized supply system. These reforms helped to create a more efficient and effective fighting force that could respond quickly to threats to the empire. They also helped to create a sense of loyalty among soldiers to their commanders and the state, which was important in maintaining the stability of the Roman Republic.

It was beautiful - it always was. Right now, he had a view of the star LOGLA. On the approach he'd admired its brilliance, the way the plasma arced and danced on its surface. That was before he'd spoken to it. The initial communications had been halting, uncertain. Stars had very different minds than humans, in many ways. It'd taken thousands of years to realize they were even capable of thought. It had taken hundreds to decipher their thoughts. The stars, it turned out, had similar difficulties understanding us. We were motes of dust to them, insignificant in the passage of time. The stars - communicating on their own medium still largely inaccessible to us, the'sea' as they called it - had debated the significance of humans ever since we'd left our atmosphere. The lines between the animate and the inanimate had been blurred. Stars saw all things as living, in some sense - some more so than others, of course. Stars did not quite propagate, or survive. They simply..... were, until they weren't. And they thought for that entire time. To the stars, it turns out, they'd just assumed we were intelligent. They assumed all things were intelligent. Perhaps not capable of communication or comprehension, but still possibly thinking on some plane of existence. "They are, therefore they think." It was a compelling point of view, all things considered. If we could talk to stars, why not to other things? Aquinas sighed, as he shifted in his chair to get back up. Only a moment's rest. The basic politics has been discussed, the nature of stars, what they wanted and did not want..... it had been largely business. There'd been moments of insight and true talk, here and there, but for the most part it was the simple procedure of extraterrestrial contact the System's scientists had sorted out centuries before. Stars were independent bodies, but didn't much care about anything else - they felt no pain, and did not care what installations we built around them, or how we traversed them. The only thing they requested was that they be allowed to think, as long as possible. Aquinas rose from his chair, and crossed the room. The auxiliary controls in his room had been another nice touch. Built for emergencies, but..... it's not like what he was about to do could hurt. He reached down, fiddled with some controls - that transmitted very complicated directions to a very big machine on the ship - and was linked into the communication medium, a swirling ball of plasma that was magnetically controlled to produce new shapes, configurations, and energy patterns. After a moment in silence, standing over the controls, bowed with his hands flat against the surface of the countertop, he spoke up. "Logla, you listening?" He asked. The star had no name. No stars did. It had agreed on one, however, given the nature of human communication. So it had been decided to name it Logla, and the star agreed that when we said Logla, it would answer. And it did. "I'm here, Aquinas." He piqued up at this, as he always did. It recognized him, despite the communication medium - and the fact he hadn't said much of note. There was some other means of identification..... which was surprising, given stars had no need for such identification. A quick learner, it seemed. "What thoughts do we have to attend to?" Aquinas chuckled. Stars did little else but think, so Logla had an issue phrasing any activity as something other than thinking. It understood the activities, well enough, but it just preferred not to speak of them in human terms. "Nothing to attend to, today, Logla. I just wanted to think together." A soft humming came from the speaker. This indicated the star was processing, preparing to vocalize thoughts. A very human mannerism. Eventually, Logla spoke up. "This sounds agreeable. It is something stars do often, and enjoy." "Enjoy? You don't talk about emotion a lot, Logla. To be honest..." Aquinas pondered whether to continue, but shrugged and went on anyway. "We weren't quite sure you felt things like we did. You know, felt them as much." The star hummed again. "Most likely not, Aquinas. But we still feel. Feeling is just another form of thinking, after all." Aquinas smiled. "That's one way of putting it," Aquinas sat back down in his chair, no longer nervous about how poorly unsupervised contact might go. Logla was a very nice star, so far. It was pretty damn unlikely he'd upset it. He wasn't even sure what could. At this thought, Aquinas sat, tapped his chin, then pressed the button to continue speaking. "What makes you feel, Logla? And what do you feel?" The star hummed, for a long time. At least a minute. This was unusual - most thoughts took stars very little time, because they had very, very big brains. Finally, the star continued, "Everything makes me feel, Aquinas. How could it not? Stars have a long time to think..... and with a long time, everything becomes worth thinking about," The star hummed shortly, then continued, "I feel..... happy. Sad. Curious." Aquinas raised an eyebrow. "Not afraid? Not angry?" "Those are unintelligible to me. Rethink your thoughts for me, Aquinas?" This was a fun oddity of inter-species communication. Stars rarely did not understand each other, they had learned - it was only external interference that caused issues with communication. Logla did not quite understand the idea of'untranslatable' concepts yet - but it very well understood interference, and just acted like it was that. "Well, anger..... it's..... when something is wrong. Or when something endangers you. Do you ever feel so strongly, you want to..." Aquinas realized that there wasn't really much the star could do, or want to do. Stars could not move. They could not act. They could barely even perceive, it turned out. They largely existed just to think. Anger would be meaningless for them..... they couldn't act out. And fear..... they couldn't retreat. Aquinas paused, and shook his head. "I'm sorry, Logla. I don't think there's a way to rethink that thought without interference." A soft humming, then Logla replied, "That's okay, Aquinas. I understand, though I am curious and sad." "Sad?" Aquinas rested his face on his arm, holding his button down with the other hand. "Why, Logla?" "I wish I could understand. Curiosity that goes without answer..... it causes sadness. A wish things were different," Logla spoke slowly, far more slowly than normal. "Curiosity answered brings happiness." "That's all?" Aquinas asked, quietly. "You feel happiness and sadness only then?" "No..... We feel happiness to know. We enjoy thinking. And some things are pleasing to think about. While others..... we feel sadness to confront. And some things are sad to think about," Logla's speech was very slow now. "Some things are both." "I understand. We feel similarly. We call it'bittersweet'. I have no idea if that thought will be conveyed right, but..... it's a pairing of opposites. Like dark and light, at once." Stars understood light very well. "It seems contradictory, but..." "But it isn't. I understand. The thought conveyed poorly, but I think the thought too. There are many experiences that bring both happiness and sadness. Like you." Aquinas nodded, quietly. The gesture would be translated by the machine, but he still reaffirmed it, and said, "Yes. Like you too." "Aquinas, we - I - are happy to know you exist. That you think like we do. And that we can speak. There have been so few..... so few that can speak to us, besides us," The star said, and Aquinas nodded. The stars had mentioned other people that spoke to stars. They hadn't said much about them, but it was much more than mankind had expected to hear. We'd assumed stars were the only non-Earth intelligence. "We love thinking new thoughts. We love the curiosity it brings to know something we can't think is there. But we feel sad about it..... to know that we can't think it, ever. And we feel sad when they leave." "Leave?" Aquinas asked, his own curiosity now burning. "Leave. Stars..... we think a long time. Even as we die, we think. A star's light goes out long before their thinking does. Their thinking slows, their part in the sea fades, but they are there. We are there. We have watched many like you leave us..... and you leave us so quickly. So suddenly..." The star hummed, and this time, the note was different, a rich and deep tone. Aquinas listened to the star's song, for a few seconds, but it stopped abruptly as the song continued. "We wish you could be with us for longer. That you could think like us. But to do so would mean you do not think as yourselves..... and that is what we love to hear about..." The star hummed again, and this time, the countertop thrummed as it resonated with the note. Aquinas' bones sang along with the note. "To think about your time, compared to our time..... that is the greatest thought of sadness we stars have." Aquinas wiped away a tear from his face. The immensity of a star's life..... it was unthinkable, how many peoples it must have watched go extinct, and yearned to hear from, one more time. "Us too, Logla. We both wish for more time." "All who think do," Logla said, then hummed quietly, while Aquinas sat, and listened to its song.

article: Pharmacist here. First of all, caffeine has a few different ways that it works so that complicates all the following explanations even further. This is the case for MANY drugs and has to do with genetics and tolerance due to enzyme induction. (Okay, left the ELI5 track for a second.) There is a fairly new speciality in pharmacy (yes, there are pharmacists who specialize) called pharmacogenomics which studies these differences with the hope of better matching patients to drugs. (Blood pressure meds can have wildly different effects from patient to patient. That's why there are still so many different ones on the market.) Someday, we'll be able to use a person's genome to help physicians prescribe the proper drug rather than use the hit-and-miss method used now. Also, drugs can be designed for certain genotypes. (People with a certain gene or set of genes.) Resistance to certain drugs or unexpected effects from certain drugs are usually inherited. But even within a certain family, people maybe affected differently by the same drug at the same concentration. Also, people can become more tolerant to a drug if they are exposed to it a lot over time. This involves the liver and kidneys, which are the two major ways a drug is removed from the blood and therefore from the body. So, yes, people have different brain chemistry but some of the answers on here make it sound as though we're all wildly different in brain chemistry and that's just not true. There are subtle differences and some of them are physical rather than chemical. A drug must cross the blood-brain barrier (BBB) to get into the nervous system. This barrier is a defense and the more "oily" a drug is, the easier it is for it to cross. (nonpolar vs. polar) A small difference in the effectiveness of the BBB can make a big difference in how much of a certain drug gets through. Also, the permeability of different parts of the brain to certain drugs can make a difference in which parts of the brain are most affected by a drug. Is it the reticular formation, which plays a big role in wakefulness? Is it the hippocampus, which is the major brain structure dealing with memory? Etc. And everyone is also right in that all of these things can change as we age. It seems nothing in the body undergoes more changes from birth to elderly death than the central nervous system. Every time we learn something new it changes a tiny part of our brain and who knows what kind of longterm or "butterfly" effect this change could cause? Damn, I love neurology!

article: Modern CPUs have a lot of things built into the chip. You've got memory controllers, PCI Express controllers, USB controllers, graphics chips and all sorts of other things. Motherboards need to have a lot of connectivity options to support all of these features, so they typically have several different types of connectors on-board. Here are some of the most common connectors found on modern motherboards: - ATX power connector: This large connector supplies power to the motherboard from the power supply unit. It's usually located on the right-hand side of the board near the top. - CPU power connector (s): These smaller connectors provide additional power to the CPU. Depending on the motherboard, there may be one or two of these connectors. - DIMM slots: These slots are used to install RAM modules on the motherboard. - PCI Express slots: These slots are used to install expansion cards such as graphics cards, sound cards, and network cards. - SATA connectors: These connectors are used to connect storage devices such as hard drives and solid state drives. - USB headers: These connectors are used to attach USB ports to the motherboard. They are often located near the bottom of the board. - Front panel headers: These connectors are used to connect the power button, reset button, and other front panel buttons and indicators to the motherboard. - Fan headers: These connectors supply power to the cooling fans in the system. They are usually located near the CPU socket and the expansion slots.

Someday, we'll be able to use a person's genome to help physicians prescribe the proper drug rather than use the hit-and-miss method used now. Also, drugs can be designed for certain genotypes. (People with a certain gene or set of genes.) Resistance to certain drugs or unexpected effects from certain drugs are usually inherited. But even within a certain family, people maybe affected differently by the same drug at the same concentration. Also, people can become more tolerant to a drug if they are exposed to it a lot over time. This involves the liver and kidneys, which are the two major ways a drug is removed from the blood and therefore from the body. So, yes, people have different brain chemistry but some of the answers on here make it sound as though we're all wildly different in brain chemistry and that's just not true. There are subtle differences and some of them are physical rather than chemical. A drug must cross the blood-brain barrier (BBB) to get into the nervous system. This barrier is a defense and the more "oily" a drug is, the easier it is for it to cross. (nonpolar vs. polar) A small difference in the effectiveness of the BBB can make a big difference in how much of a certain drug gets through. Also, the permeability of different parts of the brain to certain drugs can make a difference in which parts of the brain are most affected by a drug. Is it the reticular formation, which plays a big role in wakefulness? Is it the hippocampus, which is the major brain structure dealing with memory? Etc. And everyone is also right in that all of these things can change as we age. It seems nothing in the body undergoes more changes from birth to elderly death than the central nervous system. Every time we learn something new it changes a tiny part of our brain and who knows what kind of longterm or "butterfly" effect this change could cause? Damn, I love neurology!
